subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are there any comments or questions? If not, I recognize the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to have the opportunity to say a few words on this budget this morning and perhaps talk about a slightly different issue which I think is very important in terms of economic performance in our country. Over the last 25 or 30 years there have been a number of trends in Canada that I find very, very frightening. For example, our standard of living has fallen since 1960 from the second highest in the world to around nineteenth. If we exclude the oil-producing states, we are somewhere around tenth or twelfth in the world. Our performance as a member of the OECD is such that we find we are now 24th out of 24 nations.
I think, Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons for this is that so much of our economy is so foreign owned and controlled that in times of world recession, in times of major structural readjustments such as the technological revolution we are going through, this tremendous amount of foreign control causes us problems more severe than elsewhere around the world.
As a nation we seem to have gotten away from the politics of the past where certain people did have visions of developing our country, whether it was Sir John A. Macdonald or others. As a nation we seem to have accepted the ideas of C.D. Howe and continentalism. I think that is very wrong. I do not believe that foreign ownership and control or our economy makes us rich. I believe that is a myth. Indeed, foreign control of our economy, when we consider the costs and benefits on balance, has made us poorer and has cost us many jobs as a nation.

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
We should consider some of the statistics. We find, for example, that about 26 per cent of Canadian industry is now foreign owned, in comparison with about 3 per cent in the United States, 3 per cent in Great Britain, 3 per cent in France and less than 1 per cent in the booming country of Japan. If we consider it sector by sector, we see that many of our key sectors are really foreign controlled and dominated. In manufacturing, it is about 41 per cent; in the rubber industry it is around 90 per cent; and in the chemical industry it is around 76 per cent. One could go on and on. In fact, in 1982, 19 of the 50 largest Firms in Canada were in the hands and control of foreigners.
When one considers foreign investment and ownership, one must consider both the costs and the benefits. As I said earlier, my assertion is that the costs far outweigh the benefits in our country at this particular time, as has been the case, indeed, throughout most of our history. In terms of benefits, foreign investment is only a benefit if it is working for Canadians, if it is controlled for Canadians, if it does pass a really meaningful, tough, foreign benefit undertaking or control test. However, we have an organization in Canada today called FIRA which is by no means strong enough when it comes to policing foreign investment in Canada.
The only other way by which foreign investment would be meaningful or helpful would be through joint ventures, where there is Canadian control, where we do carry out some research and development, where we do have some markets in other countries because of the fact that they are joint ventures. However, it is very important that Canadians remain in control of joint ventures of that sort.

Mr. Speaker, if foreign control of our economy is so beneficial, then perhaps someone could explain why, as revealed in a study on the economic performance of twenty-four countries published three or four months ago by the OECD, Canada happens to rank twenty-fourth. Perhaps someone could also explain why some Latin American countries, where the multinationals have made large scale investments, are among the poorest in the world.

The costs of foreign investment are indeed very great. It is one of the reasons we have so many major structural and performance problems today. For example, consider the tremendous fragmentation of the Canadian market, the tremendous distortion of Canadian trade when it comes to both exports and imports, the lack of R and D, the lack of manufacturing and processing in Canada and, indeed, the outflow profits and dividends from our country.
First, the fragmentation of the Canadian market. As long as Canada has existed, we have tended to be a mini version of the United States. We have tended to be a shadow economy or a tag-along economy of the United States. Where the Americans have had ten large firms, we have tended to have eight or ten branch plants in this country. Because of that, many of our industries have been very inefficient and have been very costly to the Canadian people and, as a result, have not exported. In
fact, in 1968, during a major study, the Government of the day found one example which pretty well sums up the fragmentation of the Canadian market. In 1968, there were nine refrigerator subsidiaries in operation in Canada in a market, according to the Government, which could only support two such operations in an efficient way according to the economy of scale. This is a good example of the lack of rationalization of our industry, because so much of our industry is foreign controlled and owned, to a degree which is not permitted by any other developed country around the world.
I have mentioned four or five areas of real concern to me. The second involves the whole area of research and development. In 1973 only 2.7 per cent of Canada's manufacturing Firms carried out any research and development whatsoever. In 1981, a year and a half ago, we as a nation spent only 1.2 per cent of our Gross National Product on R and D. Most of that was spent by Canadian firms. In comparison with other countries, we find that the United States spends around 2.5 per cent of its GNP on R and D and that the Japanese spend around 2 per cent of their Gross National Product on R and D. By the way, very little of the Japanese R and D expenditures are on the military, while in the United States, of course, the opposite is true. In France, around 1.8 per cent of GNP is spent on research and development.
I am not proud of the level in our country. It is lower than in countries such as Sweden, Norway, Belgium or Yugoslavia and is probably on a par with countries such as Egypt and Ireland. That is one reason our economy is not performing very well. The major reason we do not have R and D in this country is that foreign firms dominate many of our industries, and it is a natural tendency for research and development to occur at home base. This lack is something which we as Canadians must change.
I am particularly concerned about this aspect of foreign control when I consider technology in our society today. In the last year, for example, we have had a trade deficit of $8 billion in high technology alone, and by the year 1990 many people in the field are predicting that our deficit in computers alone will be around $10 billion.
The third cost of such overwhelming control of our economy by foreigners is in terms of the trade distortions in Canada. Once again, one can consider many examples from the past. In the early 1970s, the Gray Report stated that of the foreign manufacturing firms which were exporting-I want to make it very clear that it only concerned those which were exporting because some were not allowed to export at all-about 58 per cent had some kind of export restriction placed on them by their parent company. For example, 31 per cent were excluded from exporting into the American market.
Recently some papers from the 1960s of the Trade Commissioner were made public in this country. The Trade Commissioner said that in those days over three-quarters of foreign firms operating in Canada had export restrictions placed on them by their parent Firm in the United States. In 1980 there
April 25, 1983

was a repetition of this in a Cabinet document which was referred to the Cabinet by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who was from Windsor, in which he requested stronger legislation for the Foreign Investment Review Act and that amendments promised in 1980 be made. Of course, he was turned down by the Cabinet.
Another example involves the Nelson muffler company, a firm in the United States with its headquarters in Wisconsin. In 1980 it applied to the Foreign Investment Review Agency to establish a plant in Canada and was granted permission to establish a firm in Ontario. Two years later, in a licensing agreement between Nelson Industries Incorporated in Wisconsin and Nelson Muffler Canada signed in July of 1982, it was found that the Canadian plant was subject to export restrictions. In fact, page 4 of the licence agreement stated that the Canadian branch plant could not export anywhere in the world without written consent from the head office in the United States. I believe that to be very unfair. It is an attack upon the economic sovereignty of Canada. It is the type of thing which no self-respecting sovereign nation in the world would allow to continue.
In addition, in terms of trade distortion on the import side, we find that Statistics Canada reported last November that in 1981 foreign owned or controlled firms in Canada imported about four times as much as Canadian controlled firms in the same areas. Once again it is evident that a Candian owned and controlled firm is more likely to purchase in Canada in terms of its procurement policy and do its processing, fabricating, its research and development and its expansion in this country, than those firms which are controlled and owned from outside our borders. This means that foreign control makes us poor as a nation since many jobs are lost in Canada and created elsewhere.
During the 1960s there was a study conducted by the Department of Commerce in the United States which showed that American investment in Canada essentially replaced investment that otherwise would have been there. This resulted in a net benefit to the Americans of millions of dollars per year.
My fourth area of concern over the cost of foreign control deals with the lack of manufacturing and processing in Canada. In 1981 we had a trade deficit in manufacturing of $21 billion, yet manufacturing is the sector in which we have the most labour intensive dollars. It is one of the major reasons why our country's unemployment record is much worse than most industrialized states. Even when we have international agreements with other countries, such as the autopact with the United States, we have tended to come out on the short side of the deal as a result of foreign ownership in companies like General Motors and Ford. The accumulated deficit in the auto parts industry has now reached approximately $41 billion. This has also caused the loss of many jobs. In 1982 the deficit in the auto industry was some $5 billion.
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
The high degree of foreign ownership of the manufacturing industry in this country is costing us millions of dollars, making Canadians poor, increasing our tax burden and losing many jobs for Canadians. We have even seen evidence of foreign owned companies that are economically profitable curtailing work in plants or closing them down. A good example of this is Bowater in Newfoundland which made profits in the millions of dollars in this country but was closed down as a result of balance sheet considerations by the head office of the multinational. There is also the example of Brian Mulroney's Iron Ore Company of Canada. In that case Schefferville has become a ghost town because of foreign control in our economy.
The fifth reason why foreign control of our economy is costing jobs and making our nation poorer is the outflow of funds from our country. Between 1976 and 1981, the net outflow of funds from Canada was $38 billion. This was an outflow of direct capital that was made as a result of the productivity of Canadian workers, farmers and the business community. As well, there is the outflow of dividends and interest payments. This amount represents a net loss after taking into account the difference between inflow and outflow.
In the gas and oil industry alone, between 1975 and 1979 there was an outflow of $2.1 billion in direct capital from this country to be invested or enjoyed as profit elsewhere. As well, there was an outflow of $1.6 billion in interest payments and dividend payments abroad to foreign shareholders. The total outflow of profits in the oil and gas industry during those four years was $3.7 billion.
I believe I have generally summarized the five areas in which foreign control of our economy has made our nation poorer and has cost Canadians many jobs and has cost taxpayers more. We are not masters in our own house.
I would like to deal with the argument which questions where the money will come from. We often hear that we Canadians are not competent to conduct our own affairs. In fact, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), who is running for the leadership of the Conservative Party, believes that we should have even stronger ties with foreign investors and an even greater influx of money from the United States. I suspect that he is not running for the leadership of the Conservative Party but to be Governor of Canada after some of the statements he has made recently.
According to reports in 1972 and previously, 80 per cent of the funds that foreign investors use in this country come from Canadian sources. Those sources include retained earnings that are reinvested, funds borrowed from Canadian banks, pension funds and other funds that are available to foreigners. In effect, we are financing our own sell-out with our own money and it must stop.
For example, it appears that during the 1970s over half of the bank loans that were made in Canada from Canadian banks went to foreign companies. Some of these loans went to companies that invested in Canada while others went to companies that invested outside of our boundaries. Today, it

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
appears that 65 per cent of the bank loans in this country are going to foreign firms.
The other area of concern is FIRA, the Foreign Investment Review Agency in this country. Contrary to the message we hear from many people in the business community, FIRA is a very timid organization. It is a watchdog with very dull teeth. That agency must be reinforced. As an example of its ineffectiveness, it will only screen about 8 per cent of the foreign expansion in this country, because it only screens new investment, foreign takeovers and the expansion of foreign firms into unrelated areas. It does not have the authority to screen the much larger incidence of expansion of existing foreign firms into areas in which they are currently operating.
In 1980 the Liberal Party promised the electorate of this country that it would expand FIRA and give it the power to make periodic performance reviews of all foreign firms in this country to ensure that they are operating for the significant benefit of Canada. This was one of the reasons Canadians voted for the Liberals, but they have not taken such action.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who says that that is not right?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very surprised at the Conservatives. At one time they were a nationalist Party in this country in the tradition of Macdonald, Diefenbaker and others. Suddenly they have adopted the philosophy of C. D. Howe and continen-talism. That is not the direction in which Canadians want to head. Canadians want a Canadian vision with Canadian goals and objectives. They want to see Parliamentarians, in cooperation with others in the country, make 1983 the year in which we begin to patriate the Canadian economy and make us masters in our own House and of our own destiny.
It is time for us to begin that process. Other developed countries in the world have already done so, including Japan, Germany and France, all of which were virtually destoyed in the Second World War. If they can do it with fewer resources, a smaller geographical area and without the energy base which we have, surely we can do it better than they can and become a nation that is economically sovereign.

subsubtopic: POLICY GOVERNING PURCHASE OF MEAT PRODUCTS-DENIAL OF CONTRACT TO CANADIAN SUPPLIER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his budget address pleaded with private enterprise to invest and expand and to provide jobs. The Minister of Finance should have told the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), "Now, listen to this. A Canadian oil drilling company placed an order for $100,000 for food which included $30,000 for beef, with a merchant in Cochrane, Alberta. This would have meant increased jobs, increased purchases from farmers, et cetera, et cetera." But the federal Agriculture officials in Calgary said "No." Why? "Because you sell fresh meat over the counter in your store."
The federal officials were clinging to a regulation that was placed on the books some 70 or 80 years ago. "Besides", the civil servant said gleefully, "you would require a wholesale permit." The merchant had a wholesale permit. "Well," said the civil servant, "you still cannot do it because you sell fresh meat over the counter in your store." So the order went out of the country.
A little later the oil company wanted 1,000 steaks to celebrate the launching of a new ship. Again the merchant was told, "Nothing doing. You sell fresh meat over the counter." So the company bought the steaks in Japan.
This merchant runs a top notch business; he sells only government inspected meat, a high quality meat, and he employs Canadian help. This merchant, typical of hundreds of others, wants only to create jobs, to sell goods and to expand his business, but he is frustrated. Would the Hon. Minister of Finance speak to the Hon. Minister of Agriculture, that is, if they are still on speaking terms?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: DENIAL OF BENEFITS TO ADOPTIVE MOTHERS
speechtext:
There is currently a discrepancy in providing unemployment insurance benefits to working mothers who have given birth and benefits given to mothers of adopted infants. The discriminatory status exists in the immediate pre and post birth or adoptive periods.
It is argued that adoptive mothers should not be given unemployment insurance benefits inasmuch as they can systematically plan for the occasion of the arrival of the infants and make necessary preparations at their convenience. The error in this reasoning is as follows. In light of the extreme shortage of infants for adoptions, and with the ever-increasing number of married couples wanting infants, there is no correlation between the date of application for such a child and the date of its arrival. The period varies drastically and the waiting period maybe up to two or three years. The expectant parents when forewarned about the availability of such a child are usually busily engaged in their own particular regulated
workday pattern. They must then make a very concentrated effort to make necessary preparation to receive the child. This requires an infringement on their days of work.
I feel that the policy of granting UIC benefits to adoptive parents should be reviewed, keeping in mind the loss of work entailed in making provisions to provide a home for the adopted infant, at times on very short notice.

speechtext:

8.000	people in Niagara gave up looking for work last month, writing "finis" to their Canadian dream. Another 26,000 people, 17 per cent of the labour force, continued pounding the pavement looking for jobs that have disappeared at the rate of
1.000	a month over the past two years.
The ILAP Program has managed to bypass our region altogether, and the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program has been of assistance to only one plant. We ask, Madam Speaker, that the Niagara region receive a fair share of the Special Recovery Capital Projects, a share that is fair, equitable and commensurate with the appalling unemployment situation that now exists in our region.

speechtext:

figures like 8 per cent, 5 per cent, and 3 per cent. We know that the Government is now pushing 8 per cent as an acceptable level of unemployment.

subsubtopic: TAXATION OF FEDERAL EMPLOYEES' CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, an abnormality and apparent injustice contained within the income tax system as it applies to certain highly remunerated federal Government employees such as judges, medical doctors, and very senior officials, should be put to right.
Pursuant to the Superannuation Contributions Agreement such people are obliged to contribute a fixed proportion of their income toward superannuation, and this frequently exceeds the $3,500 maximum allowed by Revenue Canada as a deduction against taxable income. Payments in excess of $3,500 are therefore taxable as income, but are subject to double taxation as they are again taxable when they are withdrawn from superannuation.
For someone with a marginal tax rate of 50 per cent, both at the time of paying in and also at the time of withdrawal, the combined effect results in a 100 per cent tax rate on superannuation payments in excess of $3,500 per annum. This amounts to total confiscation and, as such, is grossly unfair. Either the superannuation legislation of the Income Tax Act ought to be amended so as to avoid this type of confiscatory double taxation.

subsubtopic: ADVERSE INTERACTIONS-CALL FOR DISTRIBUTION OF FOOD LIST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is only in recent years that researchers have begun to focus attention on some of the adverse interactions of drugs and food. Such interactions are very important, whether people are on constant medication of for short intervals of time. A typical label on a prescription drug tells a patient how many pills to take and when. What does not always get through to the patient, however, is the interaction between nutrients and drugs. Not only do some foods affect the way drugs behave, but some drugs adversely affect the way the body uses food. Certain types of medication can lead to vitamin deficiencies and poor nutrition.
A number of drugs affect specific vitamins and minerals. Some drugs inhibit nutrient absorption in the system. Nutrient specialists have developed definite guides of what foods to avoid when taking certain drugs and antibiotics. This list is available and very comprehensive, but has not been widely distributed.
I would ask that the Department of National Health and Welfare make it mandatory that such lists be supplied to doctors and pharmacists all across Canada, and to make the information available to all people who either buy drugs over the counter or by prescription. This information should, as well, be part of the labelling.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PERSONAL IMPORT EXEMPTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is quoted in an article in The Toronto Star as saying there is no consumer tax break because we would just blow it on foreign goods. He said:
They would spend half of it-and sometimes more-on imported goods which would be creating jobs in other countries and not in ours.
That is the justification which the Prime Minister and the Government have used for not giving the consumers a tax break. In the same budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced an increase in the exemptions for those who travel abroad. The quarterly exemption for goods bought abroad will be increased from $50 to $100, and the annual exemption from $150 to $300. That means the Prime Minister is saying to those Canadians who stay at home that they may not have a tax break because they may spend some of their money on foreign goods, but for those Canadians who have money and can afford to travel, it is okay for them to buy foreign goods and bring them back to Canada. That is a double standard. It is not only hurting ordinary Canadians but hurting people who would have jobs if Canadians had a tax break and could spend money on goods made in Canada.
April 25, 1983

subsubtopic: DENIAL OF CIVIL RIGHTS TO PALESTINIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, President Reagan is quoted as proposing that the Middle East peace talks concerning the future of the land of Palestine be conducted without the participation of a representative from the Palestinian Liberation Organization. He is basing his proposal on the fact that the PLO has never been elected.
All knowledgeable people, including our own Government and President Reagan, know that the Israeli occupiers of the West Bank and Gaza have not allowed the Palestinians to hold elections. They have ejected from office all the elected Palestinian mayors except one. Several polls conducted among the Palestinians show an overwhelming support of the PLO, including one recently held by Time magazine which indicated that over 85 per cent of the Palestinian people considered the PLO to be their sole legitimate representative. There is not another group that even purports to speak for the Palestinians.
I urge our Government to tell President Reagan that, if he wishes to see an elected group speak for the Palestinians, then let there be elections. Advise the President that if he cannot convince the Israelis that they must allow the Palestinians civil rights, including elected representation, then his Government should withhold the amount of funding from their support that it is costing to build the illegal settlements in the occupied territories, to divert Palestinian water to Israeli water systems, to pay for the education that is being denied to Palestinian youth, to pay for the destruction of the Palestinian hospitals, schools, orphanages, daycare centres, clinics, et cetera, that were destroyed in Lebanon, until the Israeli Government realizes it cannot deny others that for which it struggled so long, the right to self-determination and the right to a homeland.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF FUNDS TO NIAGARA REGION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister stated that the Special Recovery Capital Projects Program would form an integral part, if not the key part, of his job-creation plan, and an announcement was made this morning with respect to sharing of work among regions. The Minister knows that in very few regions of the country is unemployment higher than it is in the Niagara region. More particularly, what allocation of funds or projects has been designated for the Niagara region?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF FUNDS TO NIAGARA REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first advise my hon. friend to look more carefully at the statistics. Unfortunately, he will find that there are other regions of the country that have higher unemployment levels than does the Niagara Peninsula, much higher indeed. This having been said, my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services, has indicated that tenders for the construction of ships, for instance, would be out on a competitive basis and that shipyards across Canada will have the opportunity to bid and compete for those projects.

As my hon. friend knows very well, the Niagara area is a heavily industrialized area. It is a great centre of manufacturing. The benefits contained in the budget for the private sector will be felt very, very strongly by the manufacturing and industrial sector. If my hon. friend looks at that very important aspect, he will find out that his own area will be a very large beneficiary of the incentives contained in the budget. His own area will be a very significant beneficiary of those measures.

Madam Speaker, as I have indicated, the Minister of State for Economic Development is processing the various projects. this measure will provide assistance to home buyers, after closer examination it is clear that it does not provide as much assistance to lower and middle income earners as did the straight $3,000 grant under the CHOSP program.

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF DETAINEES IN LEG-IRONS AND HANDCUFFS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. A week ago I asked him about the circumstances surrounding the transfer to Ottawa from Toronto of 11 detainees under the Immigration Act, most if not all of them in leg-irons and handcuffs. I wanted to know the reason they came to Ottawa and the reason they were so restricted.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF DETAINEES IN LEG-IRONS AND HANDCUFFS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question and for drawing that particular issue to my attention. I would point out to him that the immigration enforcement branch itself does not have the facilities or the capability of transferring people from one area to another who are detained for a refugee hearing.
In this case we contracted with the Ontario Correctional Services to provide that movement for us. In the circumstances they applied the procedures that they normally apply to all people under detention. As the Hon. Member indicated that included leg-irons and other forms of incarceration described. I find that to be a reprehensible way of transferring such people. I have asked the Department to look into changing such procedures to ensure that such things will not happen again.

April 25, 1983
Oral Questions REASONS FOR TRANSFER

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF DETAINEES IN LEG-IRONS AND HANDCUFFS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, will the Minister advise us why the 11 persons were being brought to Ottawa from Toronto? Would he also advise why they were turned around, to be brought back here today for a hearing? Is there not a possibility that someone can foresee what is going to happen so that the expenditure and the incident can be avoided?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF DETAINEES IN LEG-IRONS AND HANDCUFFS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the Immigration Act people who have had their refugee appeals turned down by the Refugee Advisory Committee or Appeal Board have recourse to the court system and are free to exercise that. In some cases the inquiry officers determine that some individuals must be kept in detention because they are not responsible for their actions, or because they have shown, as some of these individuals have in the past, an inclination to escape or not to show up for their hearings. The reason for the movement here was that their hearings could be held before the court system or the Appeal Board.
As the Hon. Member may know, we are going through a pretty major revision of the entire refugee determination procedures. We have worked on changing the Refugee Advisory Committee, and the Appeal Board will be working on other parts of the system. That was the reason for such movement. We are looking closely at the way in which this is done so that such incidents will not be repeated in the future.

Madam Speaker, in addition to this particular incident of a refugee being leg-ironed and handcuffed when guilty of no crime, are there not other areas where the Minister has spoken about the special officers who, on their own opinion, determine that a person may not return for a hearing and on which there is no appeal or review of that opinion? In most jurisdictions this means the tank in either the local jail or the remand centre.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to ensure that the Hon. Member understands that, in the case of these particular individuals, most had a past record of some fairly violent behaviour or unwillingness to abide by the rules. In fact during the course of the transfer here two or three of them tried to escape and had to be detained again. This is not the normal procedure that we use; it is only used in exceptional cases. Even though I find the methods to be unacceptable, they were applied because of the behaviour of the particular individuals.
As far as the other part of the Hon. Member's question is concerned, I would remind him that the Immigration Act allows a number of areas of discretion. We are dealing with individual cases; no standard rule can be applied universally and we allow immigration officers such discretion.
We also have a very foolproof and open appeal system. By the number of appeals that I receive each week, I can attest to the fact that this is a very open system and we try to maintain a high degree of fairness in the system.

speechtext:

Oral Questions

subsubtopic: KATIMAVIK PROGRAM-REFUSAL TO HIRE ANGLOPHONE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Katimavik program is specifically aimed at bringing Canadians together from all parts of the country, to learn about Canada's diversity and be given an opportunity to work in communities that differ from their usual environment, and thus get first-hand knowledge of the many facets of our country. When we ask a student to indicate his or her interest in the other official language, this is done so that we can direct this student to the appropriate language community where he or she will be able to communicate with his or her environment.
The purpose of Katimavik is not to provide courses in either official language of Canada, but to enable young people taking part in the program to become familiar with Canada's diversity through their contacts with the communities in which they are to work. However, if the person in question does not show any particular interest in this aspect, he or she is then directed to a community where his or her language is spoken.

speechtext:

Canadians who took out loans when the rate was forced to record highs last summer are now faced with prohibitive penalties if they wish to buy down to the present rates. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member has asked a question about supporting Canadian investors and a general tax cut, and he asked why I cannot support the budget. I do not support it because I do not see anything approaching a general economic strategy for Canada. The Government does not appear to have any vision of where it wants the country to go. It does not appear to have any alternative philosophy in terms of the economic development of our country as spelled out in the budget. As a matter of fact, the budget does not even pose many questions about where the Government wants the country to go. For reasons like that, I certainly cannot support the budget.
The other reason is that I do not think there is much in it of importance to small business. We all know that small business creates many more jobs than big business. So far the Government has been more content to give incentives to the large business community.
In terms of the select tax cuts, the Parliamentary Secretary made an excellent point. He pointed out some of the structural problems we have in this country because of the fact that we have so much more foreign ownership and we import more manufactured goods per capita than any other developed nation in the world. When we do have selective tax cuts and when consumers do spend their money on consumer goods, much or perhaps the greatest majority would come from
The Budget-Mr. Nystrom
abroad. That is one of the problems. As an alternative, I would suggest that we consider selective tax cuts.
I note that a few years ago in Quebec the Finance Minister, Mr. Parizeau, provided a sales tax cut for goods produced in this country like shoes, clothing and furniture, giving consumers a real break and also stimulating Canadian industry. Perhaps we could do something similar at the federal level.
As a last point on the tax cut, once again, because of the structural problem we have in our economy, we are left with a pretty difficult choice as to whether we should have a tax cut and stimulate foreign enterprises or whether we should not have a tax cut at all. There is also a good argument, just for equity reasons, to have a tax cut for low income people, even though much of the stimulus which would result would, of course, go to the benefit of industry in Japan, the United States and elsewhere. Therefore, I would favour an across the board tax cut for low income people, but I realize the problems which would be created in terms of more goods coming in from abroad.
Therefore, I suggest that we consider making a selective tax cut which would perhaps satisfy both principles of having a more fair and equal tax system for the ordinary citizen who would spend the money to create more jobs, but the tax cut should be provided in areas where we do have Canadian industry, such as textiles and shoes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did say at the outset that there are some benefits from foreign investment, as long as we had control of foreign investment as Canadians and as long as we had agreements with other countries. I would like to see some kind of auto pact with the Japanese so that we would produce Japanese cars and plants in this country, which would provide some jobs here. I think that is something we should try to negotiate.
We must also determine what kind of foreign capital we want in the country. I have nothing against foreign debt capital, for example. I am more concerned about foreign equity capital because that gives control over industries to foreigners. In my own province of Saskatchewan, for example, our people decided many years ago to take over the electrical facilities in our Province. Much of the money to do so came from the United States and was borrowed on American financial markets. Once we paid off the mortgages, we owned the industry, which is the Saskatchewan Power Corporation. The other example is the Saskatchewan Potash Corporation. Again, part of the money to take over the foreign mines was

American money, but it was money we borrowed in United States. Once we paid off the debt, the people of Saskatchewan owned that particular enterprise.
Therefore, I suggest that the federal Government consider those types of examples when it comes to foreign investment in this country. The important question is: Who will be in control of the particular enterprise once there is foreign money in it? 1 maintain that it is to the benefit of Canada that control remain in the hands of Canadians.

I differ with that statement. I quickly remembered five items suggested to us by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. We followed all five of these items in the budget.
First, we used the tax system generally, instead of a system of grants, because the Federation felt it was a more direct way to send our aid to those in small business. We helped them write off their losses and put an emphasis on equity rather than debt. We have avoided payroll taxes and have used solid public works which will have ongoing benefits instead of adding make-work programs.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could tell us how he reacts to that when those were five of the key points recommended by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business when its representatives came to see us before the budget was announced.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for jumping too quickly to my feet a few moments ago before the previous speaker's question period had ended.
It is indeed a happy occasion for a Member on the Government side to speak in this budget debate. For the last year and a half, Members of our Party, supporters of the Government and all Canadians generally have been on the defensive as a result of the problems that have been caused by the recession in our country. It is indeed a pleasure to be able to stand up in the House at last and talk about some good economic news.
There is no doubt in my mind that we are well on our way to restoring economic health in Canada, and this can be borne out by looking at the leading economic indicators in the country. But we must ensure that while on this road to economic recovery we enhance its growth which is expected to occur in the coming year. This Parliament, the federal Government and provincial Governments as well must not do anything to undermine that economic recovery.
As I have said, the aim of this budget has been to enhance the recovery and create an underpinning of sustained longterm growth. I believe all Canadians want to see this happen. Not only Members of our Party but Members opposite believe that these goals should be realized. While we may have some differences as to the nuances of policies to enhance economic recovery, there cannot be any quarrel with the basic objective outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his budget.
I would like to digress for a moment and talk about the Minister of Finance. He came into the portfolio last October during a very difficult time for the Government and the country as a whole. Without a doubt he has performed admirably in that portfolio. As a Member from Metropolitan Toronto, which I believe is the leading business centre in the country, I may say that the Minister has won many friends as a result of his determined effort to consult widely with the business community, labour, consumer groups and individual citizens. Indeed, I have no doubt that certainly in Metro Toronto the Minister has been tireless in the number of visits he has made to the communities and in the amount of time he has spent meeting with people to discuss the economic future of the country.
I spoke a moment ago about the signs of economic recovery taking place. I would like to highlight two or three of those signs which have given me the confidence that it is taking place. First, there has been increased confidence in the stock market in the past six months. There is an old adage which states that the stock market always anticipates the real economic climate on the street about a year to 18 months ahead of time. If that is true, the real signs of economic recovery will be felt strongly by ordinary Canadians, including those who are trying to keep their jobs, manage their businesses and those who are seeking work, later this year and early next spring.
There has been a rise in the leading industrial indicators both here and in the United States. We have seen inflation dropping. I understand that the inflation rate in the United
April 25, 1983

States has been approximately zero for the last two or three months, which is an admirable performance in that country. I will talk about the differences between inflation in the United States and Canada in a few moments because several factors must be taken into account when comparing inflation between the two countries.
However, the six and five program which was instituted in this country last summer has been an overwhelming success. We have seen the inflation rate drop to 6.5 per cent or 7 per cent in the last four months. June 28 of this year will be the anniversary of the announcement of the program last year and there is every indication that the inflation rate will be down to 6 per cent for the 12-month period from June 28, 1982 to June 28, 1983. If we reach that goal, which I am sure we will, our goal of 5 per cent inflation for the next year will easily be attainable if we take the right steps as a Government and as citizens.
While there has been a slight resumption of consumer spending, it has been enough to make our retailers smile at least a little. It is our hope that people will begin to spend more as increased confidence continues over the next few months.
Members on the Opposition side will say that Canadians do not have the money to spend. While that is true for the 12 per cent who are out of work and those who are fearful of losing their jobs, we must remember that 88 per cent of the work force is employed. We must also remember that the Canadian savings rate are at an all-time high. My constituency in Metro Toronto is by no means wealthy. It consists of lower and middle income Canadians. As I travelled through my constituency I found that many of my constituents have been very prudent, putting money aside in the good years to provide for the lean years. They are still working but they are reluctant to purchase. Their fear has caused them to keep their money in a nest egg.
A comparison shows that the Canadian savings rate is also double that of the United States. Disposable income in the United States is 6 per cent whereas it is 13 per cent in Canada. I suggest that this indicates there is room for ordinary citizens to begin once again to make those purchases which they have held back on in the last years because of their fear of the economic climate in the country. Indeed, we have seen some resumption in consumer spending and I think we will see more.
Let me deal with housing for a moment. Housing has been the traditional bellwether index in this country. I am pleased to say that housing starts have increased significantly over the past year.
The important strategy for all Governments in Canada to use is to enhance the economic recovery that is now under way. There has been much discussion up to this point in the debate about how this budget benefits the business community. My opinion that this is true has been reinforced as a result of talking to my friends in the Toronto business community. They are absolutely ecstatic about the measures that have been introduced which will improve the investor and the business climate generally. We have heard a great deal in this debate
The Budget-Mr. Collenette
about the federal investment tax credit and the initiation of the Special Recovery Investment Fund and the Special Recovery Export Financing Fund. As well there is the indexed Securities Investment Plan and the changes in the tax treatment regarding business losses. These have been very well accepted by people both in the big business community and the small business community.
I recently went to the opening of a refurbished landmark in my community, a local restaurant that has been renovated. Its owners are very enthused about the way the budget will help their small business. Clearly small business as well as big business is happy about the budget.
It is important that the budget makes provisions to help business because the private sector must be the engine for economic growth in the long run. The Government and the public sector can do a lot by levering funds from the private sector, but they cannot bring about the resumption of economic health and the creation of more jobs on their own.
However, we must not lose sight of the fact that the budget does more than just help business. Let us look at how ordinary citizens will be helped by this budget. Let us take a look at housing. Housing is one of the bellwether industries of this country. It has suffered severely in the last couple of years but it is now seeing its recovery under way. The theme is to enhance the recovery occurring within the housing industry. As interest rates have declined, housing sales have started to surge. In Metropolitan Toronto where very few houses moved last year we are now seeing quite a surge in sales. That means people will be moving out into the suburbs and buying newer houses. Those people in apartments who have been saving up over the last few years will now look to moving out and buying their own homes.
An amount of $250 million has been set aside for housing and related measures in this budget for 1983-1984. New housing starts are expected to be boosted to over 175,000 this year alone and to 200,000 in 1984. Those are not quite the levels we saw a few years ago but the number is indeed significant. As houses are being built, building materials are in great demand, which helps every single sector in the country. The forest products industry and other allied building industries that have suffered so much in the last year will also be helped.
The Canadian Home Renovation Plan, which has been a great success in my area, provides up to 30 per cent of the cost of home improvement to a maximum of $3,000 and will be continued and enhanced. This will help all Canadians in the moderate income bracket.
The Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan, which I think has helped to spur the housing sale resurgence that we have seen in the last year or so, has been extended another month. That is very important in the Spring season because people will be able to take advantage of the program, which provides a $3,000 grant to buyers of new homes.

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Collenette
The Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan has allowed people for the past ten years or so to set aside $ 1,000 a year up to $ 10,000 tax-free to help toward the purchase of their homes. This will be adjusted and allow people to build up that $10,000 ahead of schedule. It will accelerate the achievement of $10,000 to 1984. This will give a real boost to people who have a bit of extra cash. There are people around who have considerable savings as a result of the high savings rate that we have had in the country. Hopefully, this will encourage people to buy those houses now rather than wait two or three years.
Then we have the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program which has been designed to upgrade sub-standard housing in designated areas. The money for that program has also been increased. That, I think, is a pretty good group of measures for the ordinary taxpayers in the country, not those concerned with capital gains and other tax and business incentives, but the ordinary taxpayers.
But there is more in this budget which makes it a document to which I am proud to give support in the House of Commons. First, the child care expense deduction will be doubled to $2,000 per child, up to $8,000 per family. That means a lot to working parents, especially in my constituency and in all those constituencies in the country which are made up of lower and middle-income groups.
Getting back to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, there is now a provision whereby the money in existing plans this year can be freed up to be used not just for purchase of homes but for the purchase of furnishings and appliances. It is funny but about a month ago one of my constituents came to me with that specific request. The individual is a lady 66 years of age. She and her husband I suppose, when the plan first started, were in their middle 50s. They had intended to buy a house. All Canadians, I think, have the dream of owning their own home at one time or another. This couple had that dream. They put aside $2,000 or $3,000. But the husband died and the surviving wife fell upon tough times. There was no way she could afford to buy that home. The lady is now living in assisted housing in my constituency, assisted by the Metropolitan Housing Corporation, CMHC and the provincial Government. She is living a life with dignity as a senior citizen, but she had $2,000 or $3,000 in a RHOSP and she wanted to make use of that money. I made a request of the Minister of Finance and I got a nice answer from him. He said he was sorry but the plan did not cover taking money out for furnishings. That was all the lady wanted. She wanted a new fridge, stove, a chesterfield and that type of thing in order to furnish her apartment in a proper manner. Then low and behold we have a proposed change in the budget which will help this particular lady.
I will not be so immodest as to suggest that this was my idea, but I am very glad the representations I made, and which I am sure other Members made, on this particular point were accepted by the Minister of Finance. It shows how sensitive he is, not only to opinions of interest groups in the country but also to those of Members of this House. I have at least one happy constituent and I am sure there are a number of others
who have the same kind of circumstances this lady had. These people are no doubt quite pleased by that particular budget measure.
Of course, this measure will also help the retail furniture industry which has been hard hit in the last year. This measure will help the industries that produce appliances, chesterfields and other home furnishings.
One particular matter about which I am very glad is the proposal to make the Student Loans Program applicable to part-time students. We tend to think that there are two categories of students. First are the ones full-time at school who work in the summer but live at home with their parents. They really do not have too much in the way of difficulty getting through from year to year. Second are the part-time students who are cribbing at night upgrading themselves, and working in the day.
There is another group of people who do not have the luxury of living in their family homes and are perhaps working parttime in service industries in particular. They live with two or three other young people away from home. As I understand it, these people have been ineligible for student loans. Now we have a proposal where the student loans program can be applied to part-time students. I think that is a very laudable measure.
In the budget the Government has also allocated an additional $170 million for the job creation program. There have been a few problems in Toronto with the NEED Program starting up, but that has more to do with the fact that the officials at Employment and Immigration branches in Metropolitan Toronto have been swamped with the work they have been expected to perform in job creation. They have the normal summer and winter job creation programs and now they have the NEED Program. With the general retrenchment in Government hiring the past few years, these people are working literally night after night-I know this has occurred in Toronto-trying to make these programs work. We have had some problems in my own area of the Borough of East York, but I have been fortunate enough to have had the cooperation of the Department. Some senior officials have spoken to the Mayor to help speed up the projects.
An additional $170 million will be pumped into the job creation program over the next couple of years, which means another 120,000 jobs will be created in the short term. Much of this budget is geared to long-term growth and stability and long-term job creation. However, we have to realize there are an unacceptably large number of people out of work. This is one measure that will help increase and create employment in the short term. I might just say that $280 million has also been allocated to help youth employment.
There is one item of $2.4 billion on which I want to touch briefly. This will be pumped into the economy by the large capital projects. This morning the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) made announcements. Others followed up on that. I will not go into the details.
April 25, 1983

One message has been given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) over the past six months by the Provinces and municipalities. The message is that large scale federal projects can help get the economy going. The Ministers announced such programs as the purchase of water bombers from Cana-dair and modernization of the Coast Guard, $147 million for the water bombers and $630 million for the Coast Guard modernization. The Provinces and municipalities will try to build on this. This is perhaps one of the largest areas of control we have whereby we can increase the job-making potential in this country. I refer to public procurement.
In my brief sojourn in the private sector when the Thirty-first Parliament was elected and I was not, I was involved with public procurement in private industry. With the amount of money at the disposal of federal, provincial and municipal Governments, there is no doubt in my mind that an imaginative use of Government procurement policy can be of much help.
In addition to the announcements today, other projects will be announced in the next few weeks such as the core area, industrial parks and harbour-front improvements. I could go on, but my time is up.
