speechtext: Are there Members rising to ask questions? If not, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am shocked to be standing here today to debate a budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who has earned the reputation or nickname of the $200 million Minister. The Minister demonstrated such a total lack of ministerial responsibility with at least three breaches of the oath of secrecy that I am astonished and shocked that he was allowed to present his budget and that this debate is allowed to proceed.
I referred to three leaks. One is well-known. It was the infamous photo opportunity in which the Minister invited the press to come to his rooms where he joked about telephoto lenses. He unwittingly allowed telephoto lens exposure of pages of his budget, revealing a very important $4.6 billion recovery program. That $4.6 billion figure was deceitfully changed between the exposure and the delivery of the budget speech to $4.8 billion. The result is that taxpayers must pay an additional $200 million to save the skin of the Minister of Finance.
Less well known perhaps were two other information leaks from the budget. On Tuesday, before the budget was announced, Ian Morrison, President of the National Voluntary Organization, sent a telegram to members of that organization saying that reliable reports from Government were that the $100 deduction for charitable purposes would be reduced or eliminated. That became a fact when the Minister of Finance announced it on budget night. I may have more to say about that later.
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
The third not so well known leak occurred the week before budget night, about ten days ago. There were front page news reports of high Government officials indicating that the child care expense deduction would be doubled. Sure enough, we saw that on budget night. After the budget, the Minister said that budget secrecy was outdated. The Party opposite has shown it can change principles to suit whatever circumstances it happens to find itself in. This is just one, and I suppose we should not be too surprised.
This is the Government which was confronted with breaches of conflict of interest guidelines by Alastair Gillespie, a former Minister and the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The evidence was clear. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that, after all, they were only guidelines, they were not carved in stone. He even stated in the House that they would be happy to change the guidelines if Members opposite would rather see the guidelines more closely fit current practices.
I am not surprised to see such behaviour from a Government led by a man who uttered unprintable or at least unparliamentary words to striking workers in Quebec from the back of his limousine. This Cabinet includes a self-confessed forger, another who was convicted of contempt of court. Another, now departed, admitted dialing a judge in an attempt to influence a court. A couple of others who have fled the scene gave us such incidents as "Nannygate" and "Coalgate". At present we have an expert on sex who told one of his colleagues that everyone knows that after you get laid you get hungry. With behaviour like that, we should not be shocked by anything this Minister does. It seems the only way to get out of the Cabinet is to tell the truth. I am sure a few occupants of the front bench would attest to that.
In the 30 or so hours during which this debate will carry on, about 70 Members of Parliament will be called upon to speak. They will cover many different topics. I want to touch on some areas covering the treatment of individual Canadians. Before the business community smiles too broadly about this budget, businessmen should look at the effects it will have on individual Canadians. It is these individuals on whom businessmen rely for their fortunes and futures.
I should say something good about the budget before I comment on the sneaky and deceitful things that I see in it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Come on, now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The good thing is that the child care expense deduction has been doubled. I say amen. I also say it is about time. I want to make reference to efforts that I have made to get increases in this deduction. At least ten times in this House, on motions under Standing Order 43 under the old rules, in Question Period, in speeches, in letters to Ministers and as recently as in January, 1983, in Question Period, I have raised the matter of the child care expense deduction that has not changed since 1976. For a deduction of that sort to not change in seven years is unforgivable. Those who need that deduction are the working mothers and single fathers. They should get the whole deduction of costs, not just $2,000. A
24818

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
decent daycare facility in any centre in Canada costs at least $4,000. This Government is finally willing to permit a $2,000 deduction. A working mother or single father who had to hire a clerk to stock shelves in his or her store would be allowed to deduct the total cost of that expense, but not if it is for child care.
Mr. Speaker, there are two important changes of principle that are proposed in this budget. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) took objection to my use of the word "sneaky".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Deceitful.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, deceitful. I will repeat it. These changes were introduced in a sneaky and deceitful way. Mr. Speaker, I will outline the problems and I will show you where those actions occur in the Minister's speech.
The first principle to be proposed in an underhanded way is to freeze personal exemptions. That trial balloon had been flown by another Minister earlier in the year and that Minister was shot down in flames. So this Minister of Finance has proposed that it is only the child exemption for children under the age of 18 that will be frozen at the present level of $710. What exactly did he say? On page 14 of the budget speech, he said:
-I propose to keep at its current level of $710 the tax exemption for children-
In other words, he is deindexing the child tax exemption even though indexing was introduced by one of his predecessors ten years ago. Mr. Speaker, I say it is deceitful because when one reads "keep at its current level", one does not think that it is being frozen or that it is being deindexed.
The Minister used similar terminology in that same section of the budget speech when he was referring to the income threshold above which the Child Tax Credit will be phased out. He used the soothing words, "hold at the present level" the family income threshold. Mr. Speaker, what he meant to say and what he would have said if he had been truthful is that he is freezing the family income threshold. In other words, the family income threshold has been deindexed. This is a very important principle that has been changed in a sneaky and deceitful way by this Minister in this budget.
Another very important principle is being changed by this budget, the principle of imposing tax on unreceived income. The Minister of Finance did not stand up and say, "Fellow Canadians, I am going to start now taxing your unreceived income". No, he gave the people a little gift. On page 7 of his budget he introduced the Indexed Securities Investment Plan. He said:
The Indexed Securities Investment Plan is also a significant step in our systematic search for ways to remove the distorting effects of inflation from our tax system.
That sounds great. We would applaud it on this side of the House. In fact, four years ago I chaired a committee of this Party which recommended the very same thing. So that sounds great, but we cannot just read the Minister's speech. We have
to go to the multi-paged booklet on the Indexed Security Investment Plan. I would just excerpt a few statements taken from pages 2 and 3 so that people will realize what this Minister was up to in his underhanded way. To establish an ISIP-an Indexed Security Investment Plan, Mr. Speaker- one needs an administrator in much the same way as one needs an administrator for an RRSP. The booklet contains these words:
At the end of the year, the administrator will give the investor an information slip with all the information necessary for inclusion in the investor's tax return.
A little room is left for doubt there, Mr. Speaker, but on the next page he goes on about the calculations:
The second calculation is the determination of the portion of real capital gains or losses required to be recognized for tax purposes each year.
Further down on page 3 of the booklet he goes on to say:
Only 25 per cent of the real gain is required to be reported for tax purposes each year-
Can there be any doubt of the intent to tax unreceived gains? When he says "real capital gains", Mr. Speaker, he is referring to the capital gains in excess of the rate of inflation. If we did not have a Government that encouraged that kind of policy, we would be better off and would not need all of these plans to overcome our problems.
Mr. Speaker, on page 17 of his speech, the Minister was again being very nice. About other tax changes, he says:
Representatives of voluntary organizations have expressed concern that this-
That is, $100 deduction for charitable donations.
-reduces the tax incentive for charitable giving since the deduction is not directly related to actual amounts given.
That is true only as far as it goes. The Minister failed to say that in discussions with delegations from the voluntary sector, the Minister had been told that it was important that the $ 100 exemption be removed, but it was equally important that it be coupled with a tax credit system so that gifts to charitable organizations could be offset by a tax credit. We have a system given to us by the Government opposite which allows contributions to a political Party a more beneficial tax treatment than it allows contributions to a church. That is inequitable and wrong.
The Government had the opportunity to put things right. Instead it has angered the whole voluntary organization sector in Canada by removing the $100 deduction. This means that all of those organizations are going to incur enormous costs in sending out receipts which people formerly did not want. If people had only given $5 to a charity and had the $100 exemption, they could give $5 to half a dozen or ten or 15 other charities and still not need receipts. Now they are going to need those receipts and the voluntary sector is going to have to bear the cost of producing and mailing out those receipts.
Mr. Speaker, that is not the worst feature of the underhanded and unfair removal of the $100 deduction. It amounts to an $80 million tax grab by the Government. That is the exact figure that appears on page 25 of the Minister's budget papers. He says that the loss of the $100 charitable exemption will
April 25, 1983

produce an extra $80 million in revenues for the Government in 1984, lest anyone think that I am being unfair.
That is not the only tax grab from individuals that is contained in this budget. The Minister announced that he is going to reduce the federal tax reduction for many Canadians. That will result in an extra revenue in 1984 of $265 million. The freeze on the exemption for children will produce an extra $35 million. The Child Tax Credit adjustments will produce an extra $235 million, and then there is the consumer tax of 6 per cent on cable services. The Minister says that will raise $50 million. The so-called special recovery tax of 1 per cent on manufacturers' sales and 1 per cent on building materials, etc., will produce $70 million. This amounts to a total tax grab of $735 million by the time those policies have matured in 1984. Goodness knows what it will be after that, but that is what it will be then.
In his comments this morning, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) made reference to an announcement that his colleague, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), had made earlier today. I was surprised because the Minister of the Environment spoke at about 11.15, just after the House met this morning. What does that tell us, Mr. Speaker? It tells me that the Minister of State for Economic Development revealed some more details about the recovery program. But where did he reveal these details? Before what forum did he make these announcements? We are in the budget debate. This is the third day of the budget debate. The Minister of State for Economic Development is revealing budget information, but where? Not in the House of Commons, not in the budget debate, but in some other forum. I suppose we will have to read about it in the newspapers.
The Minister of Finance also made reference to business in his speech. He said that Canadian businesses have been battered by the recession, and he went on to describe what he would do for businesses. I think he should have said that Canadian businesses have been battered by the Government over the past decade or so. They have been battered by Government policies such as the National Energy Program, higher interest rates and many other interventionist policies.
The Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) spoke about people saving their money because they were afraid. Of course they were afraid; they were afraid for their jobs and for their homes. He did not say that they were afraid of this Government. They were saving their money, Mr. Speaker, because they did not know when they would be in dire need of savings. As a result, businesses suffer and bankruptcies abound.
The Government introduced cruel job programs that only lead to dead ends. After three or four months on a job program people find themselves out of work again and perhaps not eligible for Unemployment Insurance benefits. Young people do not want short-term jobs; they want careers. Unless the Government comes forward with a policy to get the economy
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
back on the rails they are not going to get permanent jobs. In fact some of them are displacing people who have permanent jobs. Some of the Mickey Mouse programs that the Minister has introduced at various times encourage businesses to hire young, subsidized workers by paying part of their wages. That just results in long-term expert workers being laid off. They then apply for Unemployment Insurance benefits. That kind of program just incurs more deficits Mr. Speaker.
The Minister is proposing continued record deficits. As somebody or other said, "We ain't seen nothing yet". The total projected deficits for the next four years are higher than the total deficits for the last 11 years. Already about 25 per cent of every dollar taken in by the Government is paid out in interest. That has to stop, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do any Hon. Members wish to ask questions of the Hon. Member who has just spoken?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member ended his remarks by dealing with the national debt. Hon. Members opposite do not often deal with the question, by whom is the national debt owed? The Hon. Member has undoubtedly read a recent article in The Toronto Star by Reuben C. Bellan with the headline "Recovery blocked by myth". Does he recognize that the national debt is owed by the Government of Canada to the people of Canada? Does he know that the holders of the national debt are the holders of Canada Savings Bonds who in effect are being paid the interest rate that the bonds bear?
Would he like to indicate to the House that he agrees that is the case and that although the national debt tends to increase from time to time as it did during World War II, as prosperity returns that debt is discharged and is paid back to Canadian citizens who are the holders of Government securities?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course I realize who is owed the national debt, Mr. Speaker. But that is the tragedy. Those Canadians should not be buying Canada Savings Bonds, just to allow the money to be dissipated by the Government opposite which has no idea what it is doing. People should be investing their savings in Canadian business. Those people who invest in Canada Savings Bonds are being robbed by the Government which allows inflation to increase. The person who invests $100 is lucky to get $50 in purchasing power back-if he ever does. Some people who invested in Government bonds in 1936 will never get their money back.
The Minister raises the point that there is nothing wrong with debt. Of course there is not. There is no businessman who does not have debt and no one expects the Government to exist without debt, but we all expect the debt to be under control. Any businessman who borrowed in the ratio that the Government has borrowed and continues to borrow, would be bankrupt. Anyone must be able to service the debt. Every individual or business borrows for capital projects, whether it be a car or a house or a plant or a fleet of trucks, and there is nothing wrong with that. Sometimes I think that I have more debt than I would like myself. Debt must be serviced, Mr. Speaker and the Government's debt is rising to the point where it will not be

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. M.A. Dionne
able to service it. That is when the collapse comes, but Hon. Members opposite do not seem to realize it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate that the hon. gentleman is trying to extricate himself from difficult assertions, but he is not doing very well. May I ask him whether he knows of any stockbroker or investment counsellor in the country who would advise his clients against investing in Canada Savings Bonds, or whether he knows of any investment which is more secure than Canada Savings Bonds?
May I also ask him whether he knows what the rate of savings is today in Canada? It is upwards of 13.8 per cent, the highest it has ever been. Would the Hon. Member address the question of any hindrance to individuals who are saving their money today, not in bonds but in other forms of saving, from investing that money in equity, especially in view of the budgetary provisions that have been announced by the Minister to encourage this?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any self-respecting stockbroker who would advise any normal investor to buy Canada Savings Bonds. I will give the Minister some credit however. I did advise my mother to invest in Canada Savings Bonds, but she is 85 years old. She is not looking too far ahead and she needs liquid capital. She needs security, not long-term growth. The only individuals in Canada who should ever invest in Canada Savings Bonds are those who need short-term security of capital-a short-term home for interest-bearing securities.
As far as the rate of savings is concerned, the Minister says it is 13.8 per cent. I knew it was very high and I explained why that was so. Those who are working are afraid they are going to join the ranks of the unemployed. They are afraid of what the Government is going to do to them. That is why the rate of savings is so high. The Government ought to be ashamed that the rate of savings in that kind of security is high. Canadians should be encouraged to invest in the country and make their savings work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my last question to the Hon. Member is whether he has read the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to put before the House some of my views concerning the federal budget introduced by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
I listened to the last speaker very carefully. I hope the Hon. Member will stick to giving financial advice to his mother!
I should like to comment on the measures announced by the Minister, particularly those designed to generate jobs. While 1 know that Hon. Members are concerned about the tragically high levels of unemployment in the country, few areas have been hit as hard as the Miramichi area of New Brunswick which I have the honour to represent.
There are a number of reasons for the high unemployment in our region and I am pleased to see that the Minister has
taken steps to address some of them. The Miramichi economy has been sustained by two principal sources of employment over the years. The first, and by far the most important, is the pulp and paper industry and the forest industry generally. This industry has been among the hardest hit by the severe recession in the western industrialized world. A significant fall in pulp and paper prices, severe decline in consumption, complicated by devaluation by a major competitor, have all combined to bring this industry to the brink of disaster. The industry itself has taken steps to reduce costs and become more competitive and that, of course, is all to the good. Markets have begun to improve. Most of the factors which lead to the layoffs in this industry were foreign induced, however, and therefore most of the solutions will also come from abroad.
There are, however, steps which the Government can take to hasten the recovery and to make it a more sustained one. The Minister has included in his budget two initiatives which will assist in the recovery and the provision of jobs in the Miramichi. As a result of high interest rates and declining sales, the balance sheets of many of the firms in the pulp and paper sector have taken a beating. Any increased cash flow as a result of firmer prices and sales would go to paying down vastly higher debt loads than normal. A number of the tax incentives announced by the Minister will permit a faster restoration of healthy balance sheets and a more rapid recall of the thousands of workers who have been laid off during the past two years. As well, in announcing increased outlays of capital projects, the Minister can assist in the effort to make industries in the Miramichi more competitive.
I have been working in co-operation with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to ensure the construction of new port facilities in the Newcastle-Chatham area. I am confident that the announcement of new funds allocated for capital works will mean that these facilities will be commenced this year. The construction of these facilities alone will mean a significant reduction in costs for Miramichi and area pulp and paper producers, and will most assuredly lead to new jobs as well as the maintenance of existing employment. When this investment in port facilities occurs, Mr. Speaker, it will mean that this Government has invested somewhere between $25 million and $30 million in an increased navigational system for the Miramichi.
It is my belief that the combination of the tax changes announced by the Minister, plus the allocated funds for capital construction, could lead in the near future not only to the rehiring of previously laid off workers but to significant new investment in the pulp and paper industry in the Miramichi, investment which would help to diversify and upgrade the product shipped from our area and to make us less vulnerable to the peaks and valleys of this industry. I believe there are also incentives in the budget which will help the mining and
April 25, 1983

mineral companies to reverse the situation in which they have found themselves in the last few years, and I hope that Noran-da, and the owner of Heath steel mines, which has announced major lay-offs for the end of this month, will take a new look at the situation under the terms and provisions of the budget and other existing incentives provided by Government to keep facilities such as these functioning, in the hope that this company also will be able to find a way to keep that mill open and its people employed.
There is one comment I would like to make with regard to the Minister's announcement of a Committee under the chairmanship of the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) to avoid delays in implementing newly announced projects. While I welcome the creation of this Committee, I must caution the Minister that eternal vigilance will be necessary to avoid the mounds of red tape which have accumulated in the federal bureaucracy over the years. In my opinion, red tape and interminable studies are two of the greatest stumbling blocks to solving problems with respect to the provision of employment. While I applaud the Minister's intentions, I am sure he will understand that I will reserve a standing ovation until I witness actual performance.
The second sustaining employment factor in my area, Mr. Speaker, has largely been the presence and investment of the federal Government there. I spoke a moment ago of the $25 million to $30 million investment in port and navigational improvements. Besides that, of course, we have benefited largely from the job-creation projects which the Government has designed over the years. We have in our riding a major military base, and I would like to comment briefly on that. That is proving to be a very difficult problem which, if it is not solved, will help to worsen the unemployment situation. I am referring, of course, to the Government's rather poorly timed, unwise and in fact unnecessary decision to stand down the 416 Squadron at CFB Chatham at the end of 1984. It is difficult for me, as an Hon. Member from a district with unemployment approaching 50 per cent, to explain how the Government can announce measures to increase employment in the Armed Forces as a job-creation measure while generating unemployment in one of the hardest hit regions of the country as a result of actions having to do with the same Armed Forces. It is imperative, therefore, during the next few weeks-and I emphasize "weeks", Mr. Speaker, I am not saying months-as Ministers make decisions on projects to aid in the national recovery plan, that they not forget the special obligation they have to the residents of the Miramichi. As the Member of Parliament from this area, I can assure the House that I will continue to remind my colleagues of this special obligation for as long as I represent my electors. I am convinced that the Government will respond to its commitments and work with me to broaden the economic base of the Miramichi region. However, we need some concrete evidence of that commitment, and we need it without further delay. The Minister of Finance has taken some action in his budget which will help in this regard. I caution my colleagues, however, that the people of the Miramichi, and I as their elected Member, will measure
The Budget-Mr. McLean
this Government's commitments by its actions rather than its words.	f
A new prison is under construction at Renous, the site of another former military establishment. It is making progress and, of course, I welcome that. In fact, 1 must say that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), in my opinion, has been a "doer" rather than just a "sayer". I appreciate his efforts and his co-operation. However, vis-a-vis CFB Chatham, it has been now some 18 months since the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) made the announcement with respect to the 416 Squadron. In that time the Minister has announced that the Department's directorate of pay services will be transferred to Chatham. That will provide 350 much needed jobs. We of the Miramichi appreciate this move, but it still leaves 1,150 positions to be replaced. Those are 1,150 military positions, not civilian. Whether they are replaced with military or civilian personnel makes little difference to me, but the fact they must be replaced makes a great deal of difference. Our patience is wearing thin. It is time for some decisive action with concrete results. I sense that in the budget there are means and mechanisms to resolve problems such as CFB Chatham, to cut through the red tape and get it done. I remind the Government again that this is a problem of the Government's own making. I expect to see these provisions used forthwith to effect solutions and to provide desperately needed employment.
I shall be voting for this budget, Mr. Speaker, because it is a good budget. In fact, it is one of the best I have seen since I have been here. The provisions can be used to bring relief for hard hit areas. No Member elected under our system looks for opportunities to vote against the Party or the Government he is elected to support, and our system demands loyalty to sustain stability in Government. I shall stand or fall politically as a Liberal. I was elected as a Liberal and I shall remain one. But I was sent here-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No ambition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -to represent the electors of Northumberland-Miramichi. I notice the hens yonder are starting to cackle again. Obviously they do not understand what a bit of loyalty means.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are laughing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is to the
electors of Northumberland-Miramichi that I owe and willingly dedicate my first loyalty and I always will, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are there Hon. members rising to ask questions? If not, I recognize the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering into this budget debate I do so in concurrence with the amendment before the House to the effect that this House condemns the Government and rejects the budget for its failure to

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. McLean
address adequately the human tragedy of unemployment. It goes on to speak about the unmanageable deficit and the greater tax burden on Canadians.
In entering the debate let me identify with the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), who spoke to one particular aspect, namely, the removal of the $100 charitable deduction. He spoke of it as a tax grab on the part of the Government as it pretends to be helping the voluntary sector. Earlier today in Question Period, in response to questions by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), we heard the Minister trying to persuade the House that somehow, in ignoring the give and take tax proposals and in somehow removing the $100 tax deduction, he was giving an incentive to Canadians by allowing them to file receipts. We also heard him arguing that the voluntary sector had done fairly well in Canada, and that somehow by having all its proposals ignored it had been encouraged.
In these few moments, as Opposition spokesperson for the Department of the Secretary of State I want to lay before the House the failure of this Government with relation to any effective measure in support of the voluntary sector. Let me begin not just by referring to the leaders of the national voluntary agencies of Canada, the 100 major agencies, but rather by referring to my own riding and sharing with Members of the House comments which come from Ernie Ginsler, President of the Waterloo Region Social Planning Council. His reaction to the Government's proposal as it relates to the voluntary sector was as follows.
According to him there are no job creation rules set out for the voluntary sector. Make-work projects lack creativity. The cost effectiveness of the voluntary sector continues to be ignored by this big spending Government. He then went on to say that the documented effectiveness of the give and take tax proposals was ignored. The large capital public works projects which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said he was moving up from the end of the decade may create work for some of today's unemployed, but in his estimate it will be at the cost of greater unemployment at the end of the 1980s. He then went on to say that in seeking to motivate the voluntary sector in that part of southwestern Ontario, he sees no acknowledgement of the fact that 50 weeks of UIC benefits is not good enough in this economy. Community support services are already stretched to the breaking point by the imposition of six and five on the social service section of the Established Programs Financing Agreement, and the federal Government is merely shifting the load of the whole UIC exhaustee problem to another level of Government, namely, the municipal level. He ended his comments by saying that this Government quite clearly has demonstrated absolutely no understanding of the complexity of the services delivered by the voluntary sector into the life of Canada. With this, Mr. Speaker, I concur.
I want to remind the House that in Committee, in public utterances, and in the House, the Government has been indicating that it intended to take seriously the proposals and the input of the voluntary sector. On March 2, 1983 I wrote to
the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), and I want to share with the House the contents of that letter in which I outlined my Party's willingness to work with the Government in laying incentives before the voluntary sector. I said:
As I told you during the Proceedings of the Standing Committee on Culture and Communications, on November 23, 1982, and as I have subsequently underlined in Question Period interventions, the Official Opposition is eager to participate in the Parliamentary investigation of fiscal and legal situations facing Canada's voluntary sector which you announced in Toronto earlier that month.
In the nearly four months since you made the announcement, I have become increasingly concerned about the penalties being imposed on the voluntary sector by the inconsistent and unco-ordinated actions of various Departments in the Federal Government. Failing the establishment of a recognizable umbrella policy for voluntary action, a promise of Secretary's of States since 1976, this sector as a whole, and individual agencies in particular, are increasingly forced to contend with operational disincentives laid in their paths as a result of short-sighted rulings emanating from the Departments of National Revenue and Finance.
I went on to remind the Minister that:
I have always felt that an energetic Parliamentary review of this situation could be a first step in encouraging Canada's voluntary sector to maintain and expand those services for which it has received well-earned recognition. The current economic situation has brought another level of urgency to such an investigation. You will recall that a predecessor of yours, Hon. David MacDonald, P.C., M.P., announced on November 2nd, 1979, the creation of a special Task Force of the House of Commons, "to report its conclusions and recommendations with respect to the measures that could be taken by the Federal Government to strengthen the role of the voluntary sector:
1.	as an objective that is desirable in its own right,
2.	as an alternative to public dependence on Government services, and
3.	in ways that would enhance the ability of such groups to operate independently of Government".
In the intervening years, the National Voluntary Organizations have made an important contribution to the development of public policy in this area by identifying specific problem areas, such as:
1.	tax reform
2.	the legal definition of charitable activity
3.	the fiscal position of non-profit corporations, and
4.	the co-ordination of the relationship between various branches of the
Federal Government and the voluntary sector.
Research conducted by voluntary agencies and several Canadian Universities, has demonstrated the cost-effect-capacity of the voluntary sector as an "engine for job creation and skills training". Now more than ever, the country needs this capacity operating at the highest possible levels of activity. As you noted on November 23rd, the Federal Government has yet to recognize the need to support this documented ability to create employment-
I must stress, however, the contention of my colleagues and I in the Official Opposition, that we do not need another exhaustive study of the "situation" of a voluntary sector. What we need is a swift and efficient review of current research and experience. This would result in concrete recommendations for early government action ... You will remember that the 1979 Orders of Reference required a final report to be tabled within six months.
I also reminded the Minister in outlining our agreement that Statistics Canada finally released the results of a 1980 survey showing that the economic activity generated by the 47,000 charitable agencies in Canada amounted to 3 per cent of our Gross National Product.
Surely it is time the Government recognized the contribution of the voluntary sector to Canadian society by launching a parliamentary investigation. I outline that to indicate that my colleagues and I have given this matter considerable thought
April 25, 1983

and are prepared to move in the direction the Government has been indicating it wished to go through the years.
I received a response from the Secretary of State on March 25 thanking me for my letter outlining these proposals on March 2, expressing support "for the proposal to establish a parliamentary task force regarding the fiscal and legal issues of our governmental policy on voluntary action". He stated:
I was pleased to receive such an enthusiastic reaction and I consider your offer of participation in our initiatives on voluntary action as an expression of support you are willing to give to my plan of action.
That was the context in which we came to the budget. That was one of the expectations, one of nearly a decade of signals form the Government that it intended to take this sector seriously.
Then we received the budget which claims that representatives of the voluntary organizations have expressed their agreement to the $100 standard deduction removal and that somehow it has their blessing. However, I have in my hand the paper from the February 22 meeting with the Minister of Finance. In fact, during their meeting face to face with the Minister on February 22, representatives of the voluntary agencies made it very clear that a removal of the standard deduction which was not combined with some form of tax credit for charitable donations would constitute "an absence of substantive benefit for the Canadian voluntary sector". This action creates no new incentive for either charitable donations or the current inequitable situation which allows the rich more credit, more reason for giving, than the lower income taxpayer.
The Minister, as we listen to his comments, makes it sound as though he were removing the standard deduction only because the voluntary sector asked him to do so. In fact, it would appear that the Secretary of State has not been able to deliver on his promise. He had promised to set up a task force on the legal and fiscal situation of the voluntary sector. He had said, "Wait for the budget". The change has been made against the advice given in consultation sessions and without the benefit of sector-wide incentives, without the three-to-one job-creation cost efficiency of the voluntary sector, for example.
As one of the leaders of the national voluntary agency said to me, removal of the standard deduction constitutes a "tax on the un-generous", the 90 per cent of taxpayers who do not give, but further cements the control of the central Government over the voluntary sector by reinforcing the need for individual agencies to rely on federal Government funding to continue their activity. Without a review of the definition of charitable activity, the federal Government has essentially ensured that the voluntary sector will continue to toe the line or else.
Looking at the budget from the perspective of those in the voluntary sector of Canada, we might call the budget a "do as you are told" budget. If they do as they are told, the Government will, from time to time, give them some funding, but only when it suits it. The real beneficiary of the removal will be the federal Treasury, with an increase of $80 million in general
The Budget-Mr. McLean
revenues, a tax grab by any definition and, as has been mutually agreed, it may go as high as $300 million over a period of five years.
In a budget which has nothing to offer UIC exhaustees, and at a time when the voluntary sector has demonstrated its superior ability to deliver the services required by this swelling segment of our population, and the budget speaks of a continued 11.4 per cent unemployment rate through 1984, the Minister is still able to turn a blind eye on the obviously under employed expertise of the voluntary sector. Of course, in an effort to try to increase employment, there was an announcement of an increase of $40 million for Katimavik. The YMCA has already demonstrated, both on paper and in the field, that it could have stretched the real value of the $40 million to $120 million worth of lasting job training.
In the moments remaining to me, let me pose to the Government the question as to why it has chosen to ignore all the consultations which have gone on through the study, People in Action, Consultation 1981, and the commitments of Secretaries of State, both before the Government's defeat in 1979 and after its return in 1980. Why has the Government chosen to overlook all the facts and figures which have now been laid out by Statistics Canada and by the research departments?
Earlier in this session I proposed Bill C-233, an Act to encourage the role of the voluntary sector in Canadian society. At that time the then Secretary of State, the present Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), responded to those who were supporting my Bill. In a letter dated June 5, 1981, he said, "I am sure that you will understand why the Government will not support the Bill". He stated:
We are already past the point of determining what is essential to the encouragement of the voluntary sector and are now dealing with specific areas, such as a redefinition of "charity" and the National Voluntary Organizations' "Give and Take" tax proposal. Officials of Voluntary Action Programme are committed to coordinating the development of the voluntary action policy within the Government and as well will be responsible for the day to day liaison with the Committee of National Voluntary Organizations.
Where is that study? The letter was written two years ago. We were told that the matter was under study, that the policies had been reviewed, that my Bill encouraging goods and services which are paid for by the taxpayers would be made available to the voluntary agencies, that somehow that was all in hand.
I want to suggest to Your Honour that the budget, in terms of its expectations and politial impact, has not only misrepresented, but has also alienated many in the voluntary sector in terms of the contributions that they are prepared to make. In their presentation, the leaders of the national voluntary organizations of Canada laid before the Minister of Finance facts and figures about the impact of that sector on Canadian life, of those nearly 40,000 registered charitable organizations, charities which took in $5.6 billion in 1980, equivalent to 11 per cent of all federal Government revenue, almost 2 per cent of the Gross National Product. Their wage benefit bill was $1.7 billion in 1980, estimated to compensate 173,000 workers, 23 per cent of whom were part-time. This represents 1.6 employed workers in Canada, twice as many as are directly

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Flis
employed in forestry, or one-quarter of all those employed in public administration by all levels of Government, or all employed workers in Newfoundland.
There were 2.7 million Canadians who volunteered 373 million hours in 1979-80. If compensated at the average wage for the service sector, this would be worth $2 billion, which is almost as large a sum as the agricultural sector's wage bill. An application of this value-added concept to financial data on these 40,000 charities suggests that this sector added $4.5 billion to Canada's output in 1980, which is 1.7 per cent of the GNP.
In conclusion I want to remind the Government of the information that was before it and remind the Canadian public of the Government's misrepresentation of the proposals. I want to cal! upon the Government to go back to the drawing board quickly and come clean with Canadians, particularly the nearly three million Canadians who volunteer their time and give generously of their money.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was very pleased today when the transportation
critic for the Official Opposition, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), led off the Question Period by asking a series of questions regarding the federal Government's Special Recovery Projects Program to modernize the Canadian Coast Guard fleet which was announced this morning by the Hon. Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) on behalf of my Minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
In his first question the Hon. Member asked how many jobs this project will create. The Minister for Supply and Services answered that this program will generate 20,000 person years of employment within and outside the shipbuilding industry across Canada. He went on to say that since the Canadian content in these projects is very high there will be many offsets and spin-offs for Canadian industries and Canadian workers.
The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants then wanted specific information on the Coast Guard acquisition program, such as, which vessels will be replaced, in what areas of Canada the jobs will be created and where the vessels will be deployed. It is impossible to answer all those questions during the brief Question Period. I would therefore like to give him further details during this budget debate.
As he knows, the Coast Guard operates in five regions of Canada. First, the Newfoundland region, which covers the coast of Newfoundland, Cabot Strait and the Labrador Coast up to the 60th parallel. Second, the Maritimes, covering the eastern Gulf of the St. Lawrence, the coastal waters of Nova Scotia, the Bay of Fundy and the waters down to the U.S. border. Third, the Laurentian region from the Beauharnois locks in the St. Lawrence Seaway, the St. Lawrence and Saguenay Rivers, the Western Gulf and the eastern part of James Bay and Hudson Bay and the Hudson Strait. Fourth, there is the central Canada region, which includes the navigable waters in the Provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the western part of James Bay and Hudson Bay. Finally, there is the western region west from the Manitoba border, the West Coast and the western Arctic including the Mackenzie River system. The new vessels will be allocated to these regions based on operational and seasonal requirements.
I would like to outline what is being acquired under this program. First, a new $100 million heavy icebreaker, type 1200, will replace the 35-year old Labrador now operating in the Atlantic Provinces. The program will further include six type 1100 tenders which are designed to supply navigational aids such as buoys, markers and lights and to act as light icebreakers. There are two type 1050 tenders designed after an existing offshore supply vessel built for petroleum exploration. They will be used to supply navigational aids and for icebreaking. There are two type 800 small navigational aid tenders. A number of small shore-based craft will also be acquired. These are used for routine maintenance work and other duties close
April 25, 1983

to shore, often in support of larger ships. As well, there is a refit and modernization program for the Sir Humphrey Gilbert, the Narwhal and the Simon Fraser. All three provide aids to navigation and do icebreaking work. Upgrading these vessels will enable them to carry out their missions with a high degree of competence for another 10 to 15 years.
The total cost of these vessels is approximately $780 million. Under the accelerated program announced earlier today, $185 million of new money is being added to current spending plans to allow the construction to get under way very much sooner.
As the Minister said in his press release this morning:
The over-all capability of the Coast Guard fleet will be greatly improved with these new ships in the areas of aids-to-navigation and icebreaking. The new vessels will also have an important secondary role in search and rescue operations.
He went on to say that the program is one of the most important in the Coast Guard's history. I would agree with him on that point.
The second portion of the April, 1983, budget that I would like to address is the announcement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) regarding the importance of the Government's western transportation initiative for national recovery. The program proposed by the Minister of Transport calls for federal expenditures of $3.7 billion over the next four years. The Government's Crow benefit payments and other investments such as hopper cars and a rehabilitation of branch lines, the producers paying a little more for shipping their grain and the railways' investment of $16.5 billion over the next decade, will provide 400,000 person years of work for Canadians over the next decade. That is what can be achieved with all sectors and Government working together.
I would like to take this opportunity to explain in greater detail what we mean by the western transportation initiative which will create 375,000 person years of work. In February of this year the Government of Canada announced the policy which will result in the statutory fixed rate for moving grain by rail being replaced by new legislation, the western Canada grain transportation Bill, for determining rates and ensuring railway performance.
The Government will legislate payment of $651.6 million a year. This amount, known as the Crow benefit, represents the difference between the real cost in 1981-82 of moving 31.1 million tonnes of grain and the amount the producer now pays, the Crow benefit, which is only $152 million. Future transportation cost increases will be shared by producers and the Government. The producer will pay the first three percentage points of annual cost increases from 1983 to 1985. The Government will pay everything above the first three percentage points. After 1985, the producer will pay the first six percentage points of cost increases. The Government will pay everything above that. This is a protection against high rates of inflation, a protection that is provided to no other industry. No other sector of our economy has this kind of protection against inflation rates.
As Canada's grain exports increase the producer will be expected to pay the full cost of shipping amounts of grain
The Budget-Mr. Flis
beyond the record 31.1 million tonnes shipped in 1982. The full rate on this additional volume will be blended with the lower subsidized rate on the initial 31.1 million tonnes, to establish a single rate to apply on all deliveries in a crop year. Therefore, there will be no disincentive to increased production such as that being charged by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the National Farmers' Union or other interest groups. By 1986, the Crow benefit and the Government's share of transportation cost increases will be paid, about 50 per cent directly to the railways and about 50 per cent to the producers through an acreage payment. This is a very controversial point because about half the producers in western Canada would like us to make these payments directly to the producers. The other half of the producers in western Canada would like us to make these payments directly to the railways. Therein lies the debate. My Minister, I think very wisely, is suggesting a compromise. The payments will start with payments to the railroads and increase to the producers, so that by the end of 1985 about 50 per cent of these payments will go to the producers and about 50 per cent to the railways. At the end of that period the legislation will recommend a review process. These methods of payments will be reviewed at that time. At that time it will be up to Parliament to decide whether the payments will be increased to the producers, increased to the railways, or continued as suggested by the Minister presently, a fifty-fifty distribution.
The producers' new grain transportation rate beginning in the 1983 crop year will be the Crow rate plus the producers' share of increased costs, blended with the costs of moving additional volume, if any. Rates as always will be generally distance-related.
The Government's contribution to the Crow benefit sharing of increased costs and other direct support measures will be $3.7 billion in the four crop years to 1985-1986. This amount will represent 80 per cent of the over-all cost of transporting grain in that period. By 1990, the Government's ongoing expenditures will be about $820 million annually.
As a result of the western transportation initiative, the railways will receive adequate compensation for moving grain. This means that if the legislation is passed, the railways will be in a position where all their traffic pays its way and the railways can proceed with the necessary and vital $16.5 billion capital investment program. This does not mean that the western grain producers will be paying the freight to move more coal. The Saskatchewan provincial Government is misinforming the producers. In fact, the western grain producers will not pay for the movement of one tonne of any commodity, except grain. Indeed, the western grain producer will not even be paying the full cost of moving grain.
What will the producer pay? What all this means is that in the 1983-1984 crop year, the producer will pay, on average, 15 cents a bushel to ship his wheat, compared with what he pays at present, which is about 13 cents. This is a 2 cent per bushel

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Flis
increase. This amount will increase to about 25 cents a bushel in 1985-1986.
In 1897, the Crow rate was 20 per cent of the price of wheat. In 1982 it was 3 per cent. In 1983-1984, if wheat prices do not change-hopefully they will increase-the new rate will be less than 4 per cent, and it will be 6 per cent in 1985-1986. Although no cost increase is welcome, this increase in freight rates is reasonable.
The railways will spend up to $16.5 billion in the next ten years to improve the rail system. The Government will monitor the railways' investment program.
Another concern of the producers is what guarantee they have the railways will live up to their commitment.

The Government will continue the branch line rehabilitation program estimated at $1 billion until 1988-1989. In 1977, $700 million was committed. The Government will spend $290 million to purchase more hopper cars. This will bring the total federal purchases since 1972 to about 15,000 hopper cars, valued at about $630 million.
The Grain Transportation Agency, formerly the Grain Transportation Co-ordinator, will be strengthened with power to co-ordinate rail car movements, foster efficiency, and monitor performance guarantees by the railways.
It is difficult to know what the future will bring in terms of grain volumes, grain prices and inflation. For this reason, the Government will, in legislation, commit itself to a review in 1985. This will enable us to actually quantify the impact of Crow changes and make any necessary adjustments to ensure that changes work to the benefit of producers, all producers.
In closing I would like to reiterate that the problem before us today on the western transportation initiatives is not how we are going to move grain in 1983, but how we are going to ensure that grain goes to market consistently four or five years from now. This is why we need to begin to add the necessary capacity today. For example, the Beaver Tunnel will take five years to complete, and we have not yet begun construction. If the legislation is passed by June, which is our hope and objective, producers will face freight increases which will barely double by 1985, but the railways will have begun to add the necessary rail capacity to ensure that never again will the Canadian Wheat Board have to defer or forgo sales of Saskatchewan grain due to transportation constraints.
I just gave two examples of what was contained in the present budget as far as job creation is concerned. There are
20,000	person years in the first project and 375,000 person years over the next decade in the second project. I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this budget should receive full support from the Official Opposition and from the New Democratic Party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. I believe I heard him refer to a small or a slight increase in freight rates for grain producers. Does he call a $21 million increase in freight charges in the coming crop year, 1983-1984, small? Or let us go to another year. The Hon. Member mentioned 1985-1986. Does he call an increase of $155 million a small increase? He also mentioned 1991 and 1992 when there will be a $1.110 billion increase. Does he call that a small increase in freight charges for grain producers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I will be very pleased to reply to those questions, Mr. Speaker. The figures do look large when you give totals for a whole Province or for all the Prairie Provinces. But look at what the increase is per bushel. Right now it costs the producer 13 cents per bushel to ship grain. In the next crop year that price will go to 15 cents, a 2-cent per bushel increase. In 1985-1986 the price will go up 25 cents a bushel. Hopefully by then the price of grain will also increase. We do not know because the price of grain is dictated by world markets. It would be great if we could set the price ourselves, but we cannot. In ten years from now, yes, it looks like a large figure which the official transport critic for the New Democratic Party is giving, but even in the 1990-1991 crop year the producer will be paying only 60 per cent of transporting his or her grain to market. The federal Government, the taxpayers of Canada, will still be subsidizing the purchaser to the tune of 40 per cent.
The Hon. Members should also take note of the protection against inflation increases. As I mentioned, for the years 1983, 1984 and 1985, any increases beyond 3 per cent will be picked up by the Government, and 6 per cent after that. If in three years inflation reaches 15 per cent, heaven forbid, 12 per cent of that increase will be covered by the Government, the taxpayers of Canada. I was very pleased that a couple of Members of the New Democratic Party invited me to speak to Saskatchewan farmers, which I did this past weekend. When they heard these kinds of explanations, they were more inclined to accept the western transportation initiative.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member spoke about the amount of money to be paid to the railroads by the Government and by the grain producers under the Gilson-Snavely formula. Obviously the Government and the Hon. Member consider that to be a proper formula. Do the Government and the Hon. Member consider that to be a fair formula for other sectors of the economy?
For the benefit of the Hon. Member let me say that the point I am making is that if you applied that formula to the
April 25, 1983

price of grain, No. 1 Red Spring wheat would be $12.90 a bushel instead of about $4.50 a bushel. In that case, probably most grain producers would be willing to pay more freight charges. Does the Hon. Member consider this formula, which the draft legislation is based upon, to be a proper formula for the railroads? Is it equally proper for grain producers, other farmers and others sectors of the economy in computing their costs to compute also a 39.5 per cent return on investment for the railroads, which has to be some kind of chicanery? Does the Hon. Member consider it fair for grain producers as well as the railroads to get 39.5 per cent when last year all the grain producer got on his return on investment was 3.5 per cent? The Government and the Hon. Member want to guarantee the railroads 39.5 per cent, half of which is straight add-on profit.
He tells me that a billion dollars by the end of the decade is a small payment for grain producers with no guarantee on their incomes and prices. This is not a megaproject but a megaplunder, a guarantee of railroad profits and dividends for shareholders. What does the Hon. Member have to say about the Gilson-Snavely formula for grain producers and maybe a few other sectors of the economy?
