Mr. Speaker, it is sad that someone who has been in the House so long still has not learned what is a point of order.
We have to look at what the railroads are making or losing in the transporting of grain. In the last crop year, the railroads lost over $200 million transporting grain. The Hon. Member would like to throw in coal transportation and sulphur transportation on which the railroads are making money. It is only natural that the railroads will invest in and give priority to the shipping of coal and sulphur and forget all about grain.
Our concern is that in five or ten years, when exports increase and people want our grain, we may not have a railroad transportation system to get that grain to market. All the NDP look at is price competitiveness, saying that our producers have to be price-competitive in the world market. I suggest that to be competitive you have to be price-competitive, delivery-competitive and quality-competitive. You have to get the grain to market in a good, dry condition, on time and at a competitive price.
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
I am pleasantly amazed, and I congratulate the grain producers in Saskatchewan and the other western Provinces on the high degree of efficiency they have achieved. Grain producers in Canada are probably the most efficient grain producers in the world. By increasing this efficiency, and with the world price of grain going up, we hope, the farmers will get an even greater return on their investment. I agree that the cost of fertilizer, chemicals and equipment is going up. It only makes sense that the cost of grain should go up accordingly. Will the NDP Members tell us how we are to dictate the price of grain to the world? Do they want to nationalize not only Canada but the whole world, which I guess they would want to do if they were in power?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal budget of April 19, 1983 is really only the latest stage in the progressive and now almost completed capitulation of the Liberal Party to the neo-Conservative view that the only solution to our various problems is to put overselves at the mercy of the combined effect, for good or ill, of thousands of unconnected and unintegrated small and large private sector business decisions, decisions which are all made in the selfinterest of the individual or corporation involved, but which the Government hopes will combine in some mysterious way to lead us out of the economic wilderness in which we find ourselves. This unabashed rehabilitation of laissez-faire rhetoric by the Liberal Party demonstrates once again, and all too tragically, that he who pays the piper calls the tune.
The corporate bagmen of the Liberal Party have clearly made their wishes known to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). What they have told him is to mind his own business, reduce corporate taxes, provide more tax breaks for business, increase taxes for middle-income working Canadians to pay for these reductions and breaks and let the corporate sector find its own way out of the mess that it has got us all into, while the poor and the unemployed will simply have to wait it out as best they can. Above all, the bagmen have instructed the Minister of Finance not to ask, let alone answer, any fundamental questions about the structure of the Canadian or global economy, the values they embody or the human dimension of the bloodless statistical world in which the oneeyed Government and corporate economists massage their stunted intellect and shrivelled souls with the deceptive brilliance of their latest graph or mathematical illusion.
The Minister of Finance has been a good little boy, Mr. Speaker. And all thinking Canadians are that much more full of shame at what has become of us as a nation, a nation that watches in agony as a Government, long since bereft of courage or integrity, lives on its knees and degrades the whole notion of an independent Canadian nation through its subservience to American economic policy and its subservience to American foreign policy. This budget and the budget papers which accompany it are cowardly documents which completely

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
avoid facing up to known economic and political realities, realities which have to be faced if we are ever to solve our admittedly great economic problems.
It is some of these realities that I would like to deal with today, Mr. Speaker. I will not pretend to have all of the answers, but I am absolutely convinced that unless we ask the right questions, we will not have a chance of finding helpful answers. This is what I believe this budget has failed to do, and failed utterly.
The Canadian people were, in my view, ready to hear how difficult the problems are and what lies at the root of them and how complicated some of these problems are. They were ready for the truth, and they are still ready. They were ready for bread but the Liberals gave them a stone, that same stone that the Conservatives have been polishing for years and that the Conservatives will give the Canadian people if, in their understandable desperation, Canadians opt for the Conservatives in the next election because they, historically and numerically, have the best chance of forming a new Government.
So what are these realities, Mr. Speaker, that this Liberal-Conservative budget has not faced up to? First there is absolutely no acknowledgement anywhere in this budget, in the economic outlook or in any of the accompanying papers, of the special role multinational corporations play in the Canadian economy and indeed in the global economy and how Government can or cannot protect the common good when it conflicts with the global profit strategies of these giants. There is no analysis whatsoever of the effects of the behaviour of these institutions, which are often larger in power and assets than many of the nation states of the world. In this sense, the budget is comparable to trying to describe and understand what is going on on a football field by studiously pretending that the largest and the key players are not even on the field. This omission alone is enough to disqualify the budget as a credible piece of economic and political analysis.
Second, and related to the omission of the multinationals, there is no evidence in the budget that there was ever anything known as the North-South dialogue or that there is a need for Canada as a country to try to articulate what kind of new, just and sustainable international economic order it wishes to work for, and to foreshadow in its short and long-term economic planning. But then a Government which has abdicated its role in the market-place can neither plan nor work for a new and more just international economic order because both planning and working to that end are contrary to the spirit of letting the private sector make the key decisions. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), known at one time for the quality of his North-South rhetoric at least, has added another layer of terrifying emptiness to the countenance which must confront him in the mirror every morning as Canada's answer to "the Picture of Dorian Gray".
Third, there is no attempt in this budget or any of the analyses which accompany it to face up to the real economic crisis of the welfare state, a crisis which is not, incidentally, caused by too many average Canadians looking for a free lunch from the welfare state. The real crisis is that for too
long, the corporate sector in this country has been having a free economic lunch at the expense of the social and environmental future of this country and its present and future citizens. The bill for this free lunch is now coming due.
Yet those on the right wing of the political spectrum who do so much talking about user-pay theories when it comes to medicare, who do so much talking about hard work and responsibility, are themselves unwilling to face up to their obligations as those who have used up certain human and environmental resources in this country. Indeed, they are even less able to hear arguments about responsibility and obligation as over the years the ideology of competition and self-interest and rugged individualism have eroded our moral capital, to use an analogy that I hope some of my right wing colleagues would understand.
Those who appeal to the common good or to ethical concepts, as did the churches or the Bishops in their recent statement, are ridiculed as idealistic and naive and out of their element. We have come a long way, Mr. Speaker, only to stand at the edge of the abyss with the Liberals whistling while they saunter into the darkness and the Tories urging us to jump headlong into the darkness in the name of renewed social Darwinism and the world view of Amway.
Where is the cry for the need to enshrine the responsibilities and obligations of property and not just the rights of property? Whatever happened to the language of responsibility? The corporate sector in this country, and indeed around the world, has been successful to the extent that it has because it has been parasitic upon the natural strengths of the human community and the planet Earth, taking for granted certain social factors like families and certain environmental factors like clean air and water. But this can only go on for so long.
As the environment is fouled and as human communities and families break down thanks to the untrammelled virtues of the maximization of profits and the reduction of human beings to disposable commodities, the social and environmental costs begin to come due. And the Government cannot be expected to address all of these costs if the very people who have had the free lunch for years, that is the corporate sector, are going to rebel in the name of profit against a tax regime and an economic model which would require them to pay their just share of the cost incurred by their economic activities and to be accountable in other ways for the impact of their actions. Indeed, most of the so-called free enterprises are, more than ever, standing at the door of the public Treasury looking for various handouts.
This is what is happening, Mr. Speaker, and what the Liberals have failed to do in this budget is to challenge Canadians to face up to this reality and to decide whether they want finally to stand up and work for an economic future that takes all of this into account and ends all of the hidden free lunches.
Instead, what have the Liberals done? They have conceded without a fight. They have conceded without even honestly asking the Canadian people what they would prefer and
April 25, 1983

engaging them in conversation about what the consequences of various decisions might be.
Do Canadians want a Government which will continue to fall for the corporate sector's false argument that productivity is declining because something is wrong with Canadian workers and Canadian society, or do they want a Government that is prepared to fund the maintenance and the expansion of the role Government must play in addressing the social and environmental costs of our economic system and in working toward an economy in which these costs will not be incurred in the first place?
Most economists and all Liberals and Conservatives talk alike about the decline in productivity. From their limited point of view, it may look as though productivity is declining. However, as Hazel Henderson, U.S. lecturer, futurist and author of "The Politics of the Solar Age, Alternatives to Economics" says, productivity appears to be declining, and I quote:
-only because they have over-stated it for decades, and swept the real costs under the rug.
Mr. Speaker, why is it always labour productivity that is under scrutiny and not the productivity of our entire economic way of life? That is where the productivity crisis is. Energy use is a good example. Is it any wonder that there is declining productivity and profitability in Canadian oil and gas when the economic model we have operated under for years has called for and succeeded in accomplishing the rapid sale and depletion of easily accessible reserves?
We have a crisis all right but it is not a crisis of productivity as such; it is a crisis of our failure to husband wisely, easily accessible resources, which resulted in our being increasingly dependent now on expensive, hard to get at and socially and environmentally destructive oil extraction in the North and in the sea.
It is in analyses like this, Mr. Speaker, that I believe we are getting to the heart of the profitability crisis in the western economic system. It is not that Governments are spending too much, as the Conservatives and the Liberals seem to believe; it is that Governments have not had the mandate to collect, to spend and do what was necessary to keep up with the social and environmental costs of our economic values and our way of life. Nor have many had the ideological capacity, inclination, or insight to do so.
The solution is not to get Government out of the marketplace but, through Government at all levels and through other forms of co-operative and community action, make the marketplace finally become a place where all the costs of any particular economic activity are taken into account and where social and environmental sustainability are equal to other considerations.
Yet when Governments try to do that from time to time, their citizens suffer great consequences. We have to face up to this as well, which brings me back to my first two claims about the way in which the budget avoids reality in pretending that there are no multinational corporations and in ignoring the
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
need for a new international economic order. At present countries which try to achieve social, economic and environmental justice are likely to be boycotted by the multinationals economically and branded as suspect by the Americans politically, if not actively persecuted.
The multinationals can and do use their almost lethal global mobility to invest elsewhere when their profit margins are threatened. The Americans actively prevent that global dialogue, which is crucial, by filling the councils of the world with their deadly innocent rhetoric about free enterprise and the communist conspiracy. The only country allowed to defend itself economically, even if it violates the principles of free enterprise, is the United States. Somehow that is all right.
The three issues that I have raised are all related. We cannot, in Canada hope to build a socially and environmentally sound future unless we find a way to control our own economic destiny and make it significantly less vulnerable to decisions taken outside our border in the board rooms of foreign multinationals. We cannot hope to do this apart from a new and just international economic order in which the power of the multinationals will either be dissipated or made accountable to the planetary common good and in which they will be unable to play nation off against nation. We have to work on all fronts simultaneously.
There is a new social and economic order taking shape, both domestically and internationally, within the deteriorating shell of the system we have known for decades. New things are happening, technologically speaking and in the international division of labour, resources and wealth. This can be the greatest opportunity that humankind has ever had if we take advantage of our present dilemma to evaluate honestly, objectively and ethically, the problems that we have as a human community.
We must resolve to co-operate in building a world in which new technologies will serve real human needs, not narrowly commercial priorities, in which Third World development means real human development and not exporting raw capitalism to countries without the political culture to stand up to it, and the de-industrialization of countries like Canada, in which all economic development is designed and judged according to the needs of present and future generations for a liveable environment, and in which countries like Canada do not have to give up all they have accomplished in social policy, like medicare, for example, in order to remain competitive- competitive being the word for responding to the present blackmail.
This is the challenge from which the Liberals, with the advice and consent of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, have walked away by not acting now to stimulate debate on these crucial matters. Canadians are to remain spectators to a game which involves their very survival.
As I said before, a new world order is taking shape within the existing one-a new economic world order. It will not conform to the theories of Keynesians, Marxists, monetarists or supply-side economists or, for that matter, to the traditional

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
expectations of any political tradition. All of us in the near future will have to re-examine our assumptions.
What I have argued today is that the prevailing political views, that of the neo-conservative, Liberal and Progressive Conservatives, does not have the conceptual capacity or the political room to understand and then show us the way out. They are in retreat from the pressures we are experiencing. They are trying to go back instead of going through to the other side of the problems we are experiencing.
Nevertheless it is still an open future. As free human beings and as a free human community it seems to me that we cannot believe or act otherwise. Therefore, let us not hand over our future to the global corporate and technocratic planning elite and its political vassals, the Liberals and the Conservatives.
As democratic socialists we believe that we have something special and crucial to offer in the debate about what kind of shape the new order ought to take and what we can do as a country and as individuals to help it become that new opportunity for justice and survival that I spoke of earlier.
Democratic socialists by their very name have always held to the basic insights that the present economic crisis is revealing to more and more people who look at it closely; that is, first, that our economic system must be made accountable to the common good in all its dimensions and that this can only be done through increasing democratic control of the economy in various ways.
Second, the so-called economic realities are really social realities and cannot be understood in narrow economic terms. That is why we call ourselves democratic socialists.
We want to see a world in which people as individuals and as comunities have more control in co-operation with all our fellow inhabitants on the planet over the economic decisions which affect the social, environmental and political quality of their respective futures. This can only be done through activist Governments, democratically mandated to seek this kind of world. It is this kind of mandate which I and my NDP colleagues are seeking from the Canadian people. The failure of this budget to face reality only makes our task more urgent.
The ideological battle lines are drawn and are becoming more clear every day as Liberals and Conservatives fall into line behind each other. I invite our opponents to justify their stances at this conceptual level and try to refute what I have to say. In the final analysis I still believe it will be in the serious exchange of ideas and not in partisan exchange of competitive number crunching that Canadians may yet come to see the need for, and have a desire to find, ways to have real economic and human growth that is more than just the last destructive fling of so-called free enterprise. That is a fling which could fatally damage the long-term health of the economy and society and the planet earth.
But that kind of debate is not in the interests of either the Liberals or the Conservatives, and also we will likely continue to see their relationship continue as it has, the goal of which can only be described as the perfection of the superficial and the elevation of parliamentary confrontation to the be all and
end all of politics in this country, at the expense of the Canadian people and ultimately of the global community, as a country which has the political and economic resource to be an example to the world, Canada, shirks its responsibility and backslides into the pit.
It is this same lack of will to face up to the need for fundamental change that explains why the Government will continue to spend $12 billion per year on unemployment rather than spending an equivalent sum on meaningful work instead of cosmetic, short-term, revolving door job-creation programs.
As difficult as the burden of $12 billion is on the federal Treasury, it is preferred by the Liberals to facing the retaliation of the international and domestic investment community which would regard the spending of money to actually give people meaningful work as a threat to its dominance of the economic order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a distortion or two in the Hon. Member's speech which 1 believe deserves correcting, and perhaps we can put some of these items into a little better perspective. The Hon. Member, for example, went on about how discussions of productivity are often anti-labour. I would like to quote to him from the budget and then get an expansion on that bias of his and some additional comments. I will quote from page 24666 of Hansard. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said:
Many people are under the impression that productivity gains cause unemployment.
Then he continues further on:
We should recognize, for example, that the concerns of the labour movement for working conditions, the quality and safety of the work place, the involvement of workers in what they are doing, and the possibilities for self-development offered to them, are entirely legitimate and can, if properly addressed, improve our productivity performance.
A little further on he says:
There will always be tensions between labour, business and Government. But that should not prevent labour, business and Government from co-operating to improve the productivity and competitiveness of the Canadian economy. This is the key to higher wages and better profits.
That is precisely the opposite of the implication raised by the Hon. Member, and I believe the Hon. Member might appreciate the opportunity to stand up and admit in the House, first, that labour has a legitimate voice on productivity issues and, second, to recognize that the Government is listening to that voice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity, not to admit that what I said was wrong but rather to elaborate on why the Hon. Member, in speaking for the Government, completely missed the point. In fact, he has reinforced what I had to say. He can only think of productivity in terms of labour-management relations. The whole statement from the budget which he quoted ignores completely the other matter of productivity, which I rightly condemn the Government for not bringing into the analysis, and that is the productivity of our
April 25, 1983

traditional investment models, the productivity of the way we organize our whole economy. What I am saying is there is no fundamental critique of the way in which productivity has been lessened over the years by the way we do things in general. The Member, when he rose to quote to me a paragraph from the budget which only refers to labour management relations, reinforces the point I made. It does not go against my point at all. The Hon. Member should take a course in logic and spare us all these non sequiturs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have heard the Hon. Member talk a great deal about productivity. Could he define it for us in precise and concise terms, please?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know enough about the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) to know that he knows what is meant when people speak about productivity. The point which I have been trying to make is that we have too narrow a view of what we mean when we talk about productivity. That is precisely the point. For me to give a traditional definition of what productivity means would seem to be pointless. I would hope that he would have something more important to ask me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not want the Hon. Member to give me a traditional view of productivity. I would like him to define in precise and concise terms precisely what he means by "productivity".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let me put it this way, Mr. Speaker: You cannot call something productive which over time eats up the social and environmental resources of a country or a planet, for that matter. I am saying that only those things which are sustainable socially and environmentally can be called productive. Those are the kinds of things which ought to be taken into consideration when one is talking about productivity, and we have not done that to date. We have talked about profits, how many widgets we can get out in an hour, how the new technologies will improve delivery times, and what we can get out of a factory in a certain time compared to what we used to be able to do. I am saying that is not all we should be thinking about when we talk about productivity. We need to look at the big picture both domestically and internationally. If the Hon. Member does not understand that point then we are in serious trouble, indeed. Of course, we are in serious trouble because it is people like him who man the back benches of the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Hon. Member that there are a great many things which have to be included within the concept of productivity. However, in light of the fact that he spent a great deal of his speech dealing with the concept of productivity and how it was wrongly defined traditionally, I still would like to have him define what he means by productivity and not beat around the bush, as he just did, in trying to answer my question.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to beat around the bush. Perhaps it is just a habit of mind I have that I do not easily come up with examples. I will give you an example,
The Budget-Mr. Blaikie
however. I was on a tour a while ago in northwestern Ontario. Tell me what is productive about cutting down millions and millions of acres of forest and not re-seeding the trees, thereby putting the Canadian forestry workers in a position where they now have to go farther and farther afield for products upon which we are dependent for our balance of trade and that sort of thing, not to mention the need for wood domestically. What has been so grandly productive about that way of managing our forests in this country? There is nothing productive about it at all. What was so productive about the mercury poisoning of the English-Wabigoon river system? What is so productive about what our economy has done to the inner cities of our country? I could go on for hours, Mr. Speaker, about cancers in the workplace, long-term health problems, etc. The list is endless. If the Hon. Member does not know what I am talking about, then he has a very serious problem. We all do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member is beginning to give us some useful and concrete examples, and I would like to follow up a little further on the question asked by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). It would help the House considerably, I believe, if we could distinguish between the vague dogmatism of the Hon. Member and the much more specific and useful concrete examples which he has put forward. Could he try and bridge the gap between his examples and his dogmatism by answering the question put by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre and tell us how he defines productivity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is making my point again. I asked why do we not talk about something at the level of ideas, for a change. I know that is really hard for Liberals. I know they have to have examples, little pictures and story books to help them along. There is nothing wrong with what I had to say, Mr. Speaker, and I was not being vaguely dogmatic. Indeed, I hinted that we all had to re-examine our basic economic assumptions. However, that is something which the Liberals are unwilling to do. They are unwilling to think. They want to rise and be cute and tell me that if I do not have a long list of examples there is something wrong with my arguments. I challenge any one of them-because neither one of them has done this yet-to get up and address the argument I have made head on. They have not done that, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say to the Hon. Member, with respect to a definition of productivity, it seems to me one cannot talk about ideas when one is refusing to define the concepts in terms of the word he is using. The Hon. Member refuses to define what he means by productivity. I would define it as being the amount of output, the amount of Gross National Product, not in just narrow terms of dollars but in terms of quality of life, in broad terms, which all of us can share among ourselves. If that is going up, then productivity is obviously increasing, the standard of living is increasing. Productivity is all about increasing the well-being of Canadians. That is my definition. Now I have not been able to extract a definition of exactly what it is the Hon. Member is talking

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Taylor
about, but if he is going to talk about ideas, it seems to me that he must define what it is that his ideas are referring to.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Precisely, Mr. Speaker. For too long we have measured productivity in terms of the Gross National Product. When you talk about GNP, traffic accidents in which young people are killed are equal to anything else in term of generating economic activities. All things are equal when you add them up into the GNP. Precisely what I am saying is that for too long our way of measuring productivity, or well-being, to use the Hon. Member's phrase, has been too narrowly construed in terms of money, in terms of input and output, and the very kind of depersonalized and dehumanized concepts which the Member just used when he started talking about the input and output and the GNP. That is exactly what I am talking about. We have been prisoners of that. I said we have to get down and talk about what we mean about productivity, and the Hon. Member is not willing to do that.
I do not make any apologies for not having a whole new plan in order to be able to criticize what we have regarded as productivity to date. If we wait to get into that kind of debate until someone has an answer which is beyond criticism, we will be stuck for years within the conceptual prison you guys have foisted on this country for the last three decades.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the discussion we just heard was a private one between the Liberals and the NDP, but I would like to tell you what I as an ordinary, common, every-day rank and filer mean by productivity. I was raised in the coal mines. There was a miner who actually loaded the cars, and he tried to load 12 or 13 cars a day. You get paid so much per car. In the Newcastle Mine there was a competition on to see who could increase productivity by loading 14, 15 or 16 cars. Believe it or not, one man there loaded 20 cars in one day. He did this on his hands and knees in these low mine shafts. Weil, that is increasing productivity. If another fellow was quite lazy and loaded only eight, that is the opposite of productivity.
A few years ago I was in the elevator of the Calgary Inn. I said to this fellow there with me, "Are you from Alberta?" He said, "No, I am from Newfoundland." 1 said, "How do you like Alberta?" He said, "I don't like it at all." I was rather shocked. I asked why. He said, "I am going back to Newfoundland. I am a bricklayer. I am used to laying as many bricks as I can per day and my boss is on my back because he tells me I am laying too many bricks. I am not going to work in conditions like that. I want to earn the money, I want to produce as much as I can." That is increasing productivity, men with that attitude. If they say, "I am going to do as little as I can, work to rule", that is not increasing productivity. That is what the man on the street understands by productivity. Unless we as Canadians, together, increase productivity, we lower the standard of those who do not work, the senior citizens, the crippled and the aged. They are the ones who are going to depend on productivity growing. That will happen if
each individual does his part. That is what makes the country great. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think it is a really worthwhile topic, but I did not stand up to talk about productivity.
I want to make an announcement, Mr. Speaker. Today, there was a baby bom to Mr. and Mrs. Albert Cooper. He was six and a half pounds in weight, born at 11.30 this morning, and we are happy to say that the mother and baby are doing well and the father is enthusiastically excited.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am just about ready to make it relevant to the budget. I am going to tell Albert that next time he should have twins. But the point I really want to make-and I am sorry about this, as I am sure Mr. and Mrs. Cooper must be sorry about it too-is that every parent who has a baby like little baby Albert Brandon Cooper and every baby like him is born with a debt of $3,800 around his neck. That is how he is starting life in this country. It is increasing every time the Liberals bring in a budget and the poor little babies have a greater weight around their neck.
Is that relevant, Mr. Speaker? I think it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to speak a little longer about babies and that debt, but I have several other things I want to talk about. I think the Minister touched a real chord when he said we have to build confidence in this country. That is one of the difficulties in Canada today, lack of confidence. A man on the street in Calgary said to me one day, "I just came back from the United States where I invested $10,000". I said, "How come you did not invest in Canada?" He is a Canadian. He said, "I wouldn't invest ten cents in Canada, I have no confidence in the Government." Hundreds of people are taking their money out, investing it somewhere else, because they do not have confidence in the Government. The Minister touched on the real heart of this whole thing when he said we have to build confidence in this country. I think we do, and today. I think the budget helps to build confidence to a degree. It is certainly building a lot more confidence than the last two budgets. The last two budgets destroyed confidence in this country. But there are too many people today making fun of the financial policies of the present Government. That does not help confidence at all. For instance, an ad appeared in the Calgary Herald on March 2, and one of my constituents sent it to me. This is what it said:
April 25, 1983



Loyal Liberal Party member. Preferably ex-M.P. with $20,000 to invest in a feasibility study and pilot project to turn Alberta crude into N.B. coal. Must have suitable connections with top Liberal M.P.s to obtain a 10 million or more government grant.
Excellent return on investment assured.
Success of project not assured.

The newspaper contacted the man. He said he spent $121.50 for this ad, somewhat as a joke, because he was so angry with the Government. I do not know how many of my constituents have written to me and said there is no confidence in this Government. It has to build confidence and stop some of the things it is doing to destroy confidence, such as the "Coalgate" affair and the destruction of a beautiful part of Banff National Park.
There is another thing which is very important, too. If you are going to have confidence, it grows from each individual being satisfied. When I ran a business I tried to satisfy each individual who came in that store. 1 said to my staff, "It does not matter what you think of them". One of the girls had said to me, "Oh, he is a drunkard, he is no good". I said, "I do not care what you think of him, he is coming in here and he gets service. His money is just as good as the money from the millionaire. As a matter of fact, I would rather do him the service because he needs the help. 1 want everyone in this office to realize that. If that customer goes out satisfied, he tells somebody else and the business grows. But every dissatisfied one you send out, I tell you, it is not something that is going to lift you up or build confidence".
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have a story here that I never thought I would have to tell in the House of Commons. I am sorry the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) has gone because it certainly concerns his Department. It concerns a man and his family who are now frightened of this Government. Not only have they no confidence in the Government, they are frightened of it. Let me give you the story quickly. This man sent a $1,000 installment to Revenue Canada. The cheque was not only stamped by the Department but it was also credited to my constituent's account. Someone in the Department of Revenue decided that it had not been credited to the right account, so he transferred it. My constituent notified the Department of the mistake. It appeared that in transferring this money back and forth, it was finally lost. My constituent contacted the Department, and his bookkeeper went to the Calgary office time in and time out asking the Government, "What about this $1,000"? Each time he was told that it looked as if the money had been found and it would not be long. The bookkeeper was at the tax office on an average of once a week to obtain copies of the account and stamped cheques, proof of the remittance, but each time he was told that it was a simple computer mistake and would be corrected shortly. Each time he was told that it looked as if the money had been found. Around that time, the Department of National Revenue moved many records from Calgary and
The Budget-Mr. Taylor
Edmonton to the Winnipeg office, and all the papers went to Winnipeg. The $1,000 was lost again.
At one point my constituent even phoned the Winnipeg office, which told him that after a certain number of years the account was closed and that he should have done something about it before. He had been trying to do something about it before. He had been trying to do something about it week by week, throughout the whole period.
I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister who said, "We have destroyed our records. This man kept paying his installments until his payments were down to less than $1,000. Then, on the strength of all his representations, he figured that the $ 1,000 would look after the $900 or so in tax. However, the first thing that my constituent knew was that the Department of National Revenue had gone to his bank and had taken $1,000 out of his account without even telling him, and then closed the case.
Do Hon. Members think that we can get anything from the Department? It says that the records have been destroyed, that it does not have them. I do not care whether or not it has the records. The $1,000 was received by the Department of National Revenue and it should be accounted for. The Department sent two cheques back to the bank in Calgary, but the bank in Calgary says that there are no notations. If the Department proves that it sent the $1,000 back to us, we will pay the $1,000, but the Department is not doing that. This cannot be simply wiped off and sloughed off. This amounts to $1,000 of hard work by that man. I am asking the Government, every backbencher, every Minister, to be honest enough to say to this man, "We will give you your $1,000, because the Department stamped and received it". This man should not be out that $1,000. That is the type of thing that undermines confidence.
I would like to mention something else with regard to asking private enterprise to help us out. I have high respect for the Hon. Members to our far left. I think they are sincere in the things in which they believe. I do not believe what they believe. I do not believe in nationalization. I believe in free enterprise. However, I do not like the way they slur free enterprise all the time. Maybe they do not like the way I slur nationalization, and I suppose we are even in that respect.
You're right.

However, I want to tell Your Honour that many of the people who support the Hon. Members on the far left are free enterprisers, such as the farmers. They want to make a profit. They cannot stay in business unless they make a profit. What is wrong with making a profit? Making a profit has given us the highest standard of living in the world. We can say to someone, "You can invest your money and you can make a dollar. There is an incentive. When you make a dollar you can buy something else, you can give your family a better standard of living, buy better clothes and buy things you like. You can take your wife and family on a holiday. You can have

April 25, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Taylor
extra furniture and good food". All of these things come from hard work and investing, increasing productivity, and then the country benefits as well. I believe in making a profit. I do not believe in exorbitant profit, but I believe that people who are working are entitled to a profit. That is what really keeps this country going. However, here the Government is asking free enterprise to cooperate.
When I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) asking private enterprisers to cooperate in getting us out of the mess the country is in, I could not help but think that part of the mess was due to his national energy policy. It just about ruined our farms in the West as well as our oil and gas industry. It went right down into the stores and lunch counters in the small towns. The effect of the national energy policy really hurt the country. It was a destructive policy, but now the same Minister is asking free enterprisers to expand their businesses, to hire more people, to invest more money, because that is what will get us out of this slump, and I agree with him.
If we can get thousands and thousands of entrepreneurs to hire one to ten people, it will not be long before we have 1 million or 2 million people employed. I do not accept the theory that we cannot have a country in which everyone who is able to work is employed. There may be a few who do not want to work, but most people want to work provided they can make a decent wage and see a chance of giving their families a better standard of living, perhaps sending their boys and girls to university.
I was raised in a poor home and I know how people feel. We did not think we could ever send anyone in our family to university because we did not have the money. There were ten children to feed. The mines were only working four or five months a year. Finally, through the help of my brothers I was sent, the first out of the ten, to university or normal school so that I could obtain a teacher's certificate. Then, after that, we were able to send my sister by working together. However, they were willing to work and sacrifice so that they could provide a better education for the rest of us, and it is even more so with parents. They want to do that. The Minister is certainly tapping the right source. If he can build confidence, he can certainly get people working. This is true, provided that too many obstacles are not put in the way.
Earlier today I mentioned the story of a man in Cochrane who received an order amounting to $103,000 from an oil company. The oil company had built a couple of ships in Japan. I am running that down. I do not know why they were built in Japan, because it is a Canadian oil company. Anyhow, it had two ships built in Japan-
Mir. Blaikie: Got a better price. That's free enterprise!

-and the company wanted to have a celebration and give Canada the business. So an employee of the company went to the Cochrane store, an excellent store with a coffee shop, groceries and a meat counter, and said, "We will give you a $103,000 order". Beef amounted to $32,000 of the order. The owner buys his beef from Canada Packers and the federal inspectors inspect the meat. However, when he went to
the federal inspectors and said, "I want an export permit", they said, "Nothing doing". He asked why, and they said, "It is because there is a regulation on the books which was passed about 70 or 80 years ago which states that you cannot export meat if you keep a fresh meat counter and sell meat over the counter". That might have made sense back in 1915 or 1930, but it is not sensible today. Why should a man who sells excellent meat over the counter not be permitted an export permit? The civil servant in Calgary said to him, "And besides, you must have a wholesale licence." He said, "I have a wholesale licence". He was told, "You cannot have it anyhow, because you sell meat over the fresh meat counter". Therefore, he lost $103,000. I do not know whether the business went to the States or to Japan. I am not sure about that part. However, a couple of weeks later the same company man came back and wanted to order 1,000 steaks. One can imagine the thrill of having someone come into one's store and order 1,000 steaks.
It reminds me of a story about someone who ordered 1,000 hamburgers from MacDonalds and everyone in the place became very excited over 1,000 hamburgers being ordered all at once. This is a situation involving 1,000 steaks. The oil company wanted all of the friends, builders and workers to celebrate the great event of building two ships. The storekeeper said that he would love to provide them with a thousand steaks. He went to the federal agricultural people again, but they said that if he sold fresh meat over the counter he could not have an export permit.
How ridiculous is the situation in this country when a thousand steaks, which could have come from the cattle of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or even Ontario and could have provided work in Canada, were not allowed to be sold. Instead, the situation became so frustrating that the man said he could not bother with the officialdom any longer. He went back to Japan and bought his thousand steaks in Japan. In the meantime we talk about building up Canadian industry, we talk about unemployment.
Free enterprise will work but not if it continues to be shackled. It will not work half as well when it is handcuffed. Let free enterprise work by eliminating these ridiculous Government regulations. I see, Mr. Speaker, that your are pointing to your watch, but I have barely started.
In the one minute that I have remaining I wish to say something about the deficit. One thing that bothers me when talking about recovery is that the deficit is increasing continually. How can we eventually recover if we do not begin reducing the deficit? I have figures for 1972 which indicate that the deficit was $999 million. It kept increasing until 1979 when the Progressive Conservatives came to power. It then dropped slightly to $11.48 billion from $12 billion. When the Progressive Conservatives went out, the deficit rose again to a level higher than it was in 1979; it rose to $12.6 billion. In the next year it went to $13.6 billion, and then to $25 billion the next year after that. The deficit this year is $31.3 billion.
April 25, 1983

How will Canadians be able to face this deficit? We cannot pull ourselves up by the bootstraps or by borrowing ourselves out of the deficit.
The Government must begin to reduce its expenditures and it can only do so by cutting down on those unnecessary expenditures. It should not do so, as some have suggested, by cutting old age pensions. It should take the money from those areas which can afford it. There is a lot of lard in this Government and in its budget. Let us cut out some of that lard. One example is the metric system. It is not necessary to spend $25 million a year on a program that half of the people of Canada do not want. Expenditures on programs such as that should be cut from the budget.
I wish I had more time to deal with the deficit. While I am in favour of some of the budgetary measures, those that encourage people to work and get us out of this mess, some of its other measures are bad. I hope to have the opportunity to deal with some of the pros and cons of the budget at a later time.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I do not have to put it in the form of a question because I know he will respond to my comments.
The Hon. Member for Bow River is known for the clarity and vigour with which he puts forward his views of the world. Given the argument about the nature of productivity that ensued just before he rose, I was grateful to him for the manner in which he so clearly described the limited view of productivity which I rejected in the previous argument. The Hon. Member was giving us the example of coal miners working on their hands and knees in the mines. In his opinion productivity meant that if they could double the amount of coal they mined on their hands and knees on a particular day, that was productivity. As well, he suggested that the bricklayer who laid as many bricks in a day as possible was another example of productivity. 1 agree with the Hon. Member to the extent that his argument relates to the value and meaning of not only work, but hard work.
However, to use the coal mining example, I do not agree with the Hon. Member's view of productivity or lack thereof, in the general scheme, when one considers the destructive impact that that kind of productivity related mining has had on the lives and families and the environment of coal mining communities.
It was precisely my point that it is not enough to think only about productivity in terms of output which, in this case, is coal. One must consider the long-term social and environmental costs of a particular economic activity. That is the kind of productivity analysis that I was trying to have Members of the House consider.
The Hon. Member asked what is wrong with profit. If he had listened clearly to what I said, he would know I always talked about the maximization of profit, which might be another word for exorbitant profit which the Hon. Member used. Whenever there is an economy in which people are
The Budget-Mr. Taylor
driven to the maximization of profit in order to stay competitive, it is a bad situation.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what the Hon. Member says but I want to give him an actual illustration of what was happening in a mining town. We had a good life as long as we were able to produce coal and my father and brothers were able to work in the mine. The more coal that one of my brothers loaded, the more money he received and the more he was able to keep us at school, and the more he could give us on payday.
We had a good life while the mines were busy. Productivity increased our happiness, our prospects and our standard of living. When productivity started to decline, we started to suffer. Productivity started to decline when people felt they were making too much for the company and decided to cut their productivity in half. We suddenly realized that we were not competing with other forms of fuels.
Of course, with the arrival of oil and gas, productivity became a vital factor in remaining competitive with oil and gas. It was almost impossible to compete in those days, and the whole coal mining industry almost collapsed.
After I was elected, I remember being on a committee which went to Crowsnest Pass to see what could be done for the miners whose lives had suddenly become empty because the mines had closed. They did not know what to do since mining was all they knew. We tried to work out programs of rehabilitation for them. The point is that it was the lack of productivity that destroyed our coal mines. The same thing will happen in any industry. If people take the attitude that they should do as little as they can, that will be the result, as compared to the person who will do all he can.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-OILSEED FREIGHT RATE POLICY-EXCLUSION OF SUNFLOWER SEED. (B) PLEA FOR SUNFLOWER INDUSTRY
RAILWAYS-OILSEED FREIGHT RATE POLICY-EXCLUSION OF SUNFLOWER SEED. (B) PLEA FOR SUNFLOWER INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on April 18 is related to the matter about which we have just been talking in the last few minutes, the whole question of the western transportation initiatives announced last February by the Minister.
The concern I have, and the concern I expressed in my question on April 18, is for a segment of that whole initiative that was left out, the sunflower seed industry and its associated products, the various brands of sunflower oil which compete with soyabean oil used in cooking.
The background of this industry is interesting. It was the first special crops industry established in western Canada back in the 1940s. It has been a major industry since that time and it continues to grow. It shares a place in the hearts of producers in western Canada along with rapeseed or canola in terms of an alternative crop to wheat, oats and barley.
Under the proposals of the Minister of Transport, if the freight rate parity does not include sunflowers along with canola, rapeseed, linseed oil, and flaxseed, the sunflower seed industry is in danger of becoming extinct in western Canada.
There is about a $60 disparity per tonne between the cost to move rapeseed oil and sunflower oil from a crushing plant in Altona, southern Manitoba. Of course, an industry cannot survive with that type of disparity. Nobody will buy the products. Why would they? It would not only cost the industry more, it would certainly cost the consumer more. Sunflower seed is the only western Canadian oil seed crop not included in the statutory freight rate structure. As such, the much higher commercial rates continue to apply, both domestically and for export. This further erodes the competitive position of this very important crop to western Canada. In the context of Manitoba, the sunflower seed industry amounts to $35 million to $50
million. That is for the Province of Manitoba. It is a substantial industry in Saskatchewan and also Alberta.
The proposed rate structure actually increases the freight rate disparity between sunflower and canola products to almost $60 per tonne. As I said before, the crop itself, unless something can be done, is under threat of extinction.
If we were looking at the cost to include this very important crop-in the context of Manitoba some $35 million-into the total plan which the Government has proposed, using a multiplier factor of 5.2 times the existing Crow rate, which I think is realistic, the cost to the federal Government of removing this anomaly and providing statutory rates for sunflower seed is estimated to be only $750,000 for the period August 1, 1982 to July 31, 1983. It will cost only $750,000 to save an industry in Manitoba that represents $35 million to $50 million to the producers. This has to be looked at and acted upon by the Government in a positive manner to ensure that sunflower seeds and by-products retain their rightful place in the whole agricultural industry in western Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: RAILWAYS-OILSEED FREIGHT RATE POLICY-EXCLUSION OF SUNFLOWER SEED. (B) PLEA FOR SUNFLOWER INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) for taking advantage of this parliamentary process of going to bat for the oilseed crushing industry.
In its announcement of February 1 on the western transportation initiative, the Government accepted the recommendation of Dr. Gilson that only canola meal and oil and linseed meal and oil be included under the new statutory rate regime. The inclusion of other crops and products such as sunflower seed and oil and alfalfa was examined. The prime reason for adding canola and linseed oil and meal is that there has been a long-standing disparity between the western rates for the movement of raw seed and the rates for the movement of the corresponding product. For example, canola and flaxseed move under the statutory rate whereas their products in general do not. Since sunflower seed does not move under the statutory rate, the question of parity between seed and product does not arise in this case.
The sunflower seed industry will benefit, however, from the Government's decision on the method of payment of the Crow benefit. To the extent that payments are made to producers, they will be made on the basis of all cultivated acreage. Sunflower acreage is therefore eligible and the distortion between sunflower and the so-called "Crow crops" will be reduced.
The sunflower seed industry will also benefit from the agricultural adjustment payments recommended by Dr. Gilson. These payments will be at a level of $204 million over three years to 1985-86 and are designed to offset the dilution effect on grain producers of extending the Crow benefit to all cultivated acreage. The payments will be made to all producers, thereby benefiting sunflower producers as well.
April 25, 1983

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-CYPRUS ANVIL MINE IN YUKON. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
MINES AND MINING-CYPRUS ANVIL MINE IN YUKON. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 14 in this House I asked questions of the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) with regard to the reopening of the Cyprus Anvil mine at Faro in Yukon. On March 17, and again last week, I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the Government's failure to deal with this long neglected problem which has been devastating for the economy of Yukon.
In asking my question on April 20, I asked the Prime Minister to confirm reports that the Government had Finally reached a decision on the long-sought aid for the Cyprus Anvil mine. Even though the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) was at that very moment in Whitehorse making an announcement on this matter, the Prime Minister refused to confirm the announcement in this House, thereby denying me and other Members an opportunity to question him on the specifics of the assistance and the delays in reaching this decision.
The federal Government has done irreparable damage to the mine, the Town of Faro and all of Yukon through the manner in which the Cyprus Anvil problem has been handled. The inordinate delays in the approval of this assistance have seriously undermined the future viability of the mine and the Government has done nothing to offset the damage it has done over the past five months.
Until it closed in June of last year, the Cyprus Anvil mine was the largest private sector employer in the territory. It represented 40 per cent of the income to Yukon's economy. Obviously, a permanent shutdown of the mine would devastate the Territory of Yukon, yet it took the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development five months before he indicated the Government would be prepared to take action. That was last October.
The Minister agreed in early October of 1982 to assist in reviving the mine if the company, the workers, and the people in the Government of Yukon would meet a number of conditions. By early December, the Minister's requirements relating to the settlement of a labour contract and coming to some decision on the northern benefits taxation question had all been met. Yet the Minister still balked at fulfilling his part of the bargain. Meanwhile, workers continued to leave Faro, Yukon's economy continued to deteriorate.
This reluctance on the part of the Government is hard to understand. It appears it is always ready to provide assistance and low interest or no interest loans for projects of questionable merit in other countries, whether it be for transit cars for the citizens of New York City, or the opening of new mining developments in various South American countries that end up competing with Canadian mines. In those cases, the Government responds very quickly.
Adjournment Debate
The delays in this case are also vexing because the federal Government can be blamed for many of the financial problems at the Faro mine. It has ignored calls for improvements to the power and transportation systems in Yukon. It was the Liberal Government's policies on foreign investment that resulted in the mine coming under the control of Dome Petroleum, a move that may be a crucial factor in the mine's current financial difficulties.
Clearly the Government of Canada had every reason and had a responsibility to move quickly, but it allowed the mine to sit idle for almost a year. This unbelievable delay has magnified the problem several times over. The effects of the Government's inaction were highlighted in January by the decision to indefinitely shut down the White Pass and Yukon Railway.
Every day that this railway is shut down its old narrow gauge track deteriorates further and the cost of re-opening the line escalates. The cost to re-open the railway will eventually have to be borne by the Cyprus Anvil mine as it is the major user of the railway. This problem will not be solved by merely clearing overburden at the mine site over the next several months, a solution which is the essence of the aid package unveiled last week.
Short term aid such as that announced by the Minister in Whitehorse on April 20 is obviously necessary in view of the desperate situation in Yukon. But will this aid ensure that the Cyprus Anvil mine will be re-opened? Is there a requirement on the part of the Cyprus Anvil Mining Company to guarantee the re-opening of the mine? Does the deal in which the federal Government is to put up a loan and grant amounting to $25 million then require that the mining company convey to the Government of Canada a piece of equity interest in the mining company? I believe Members of this House would like to have these questions answered, Mr. Speaker.
What is also needed, however, is action that will ensure the long-term viability of the Cyprus Anvil mine. The Government should, for example, scrap the obnoxious northern benefits tax which has already seriously impeded any efforts to resume full mineral production at the mine. The tax will hurt Cyprus Anvil's chances of becoming competitive and winning back the Japanese customers who have already been lost during this long shutdown. The Government should also launch work on infrastructure that would show a commitment to reviving the northern mining industry.
Will the Parliamentary Secretary tell the House this evening whether any of the 100 capital projects discussed in the budget speech will be of direct benefit to Yukon mining? For example, is the Government prepared to open the road to the port of Skagway or to launch power projects that could provide Yukon industry with reasonable electricity costs for the future? If this is not the case, then last week's announcement of aid to the Cyprus Anvil mine is obviously too little, too late.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-CYPRUS ANVIL MINE IN YUKON. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to answer the hon. gentleman's question tonight because having spent a week in Whitehorse, Yukon, just before Christmas, I heard and

April 25, 1983
Adjournment Debate
listened to the concerns of the unemployed miners in that part of Canada.
Following intensive negotiations between Cyprus Anvil and the federal Government which concluded on April 20, the federal Government has agreed to accept Cyprus Anvil's proposal to re-open the mine. Implementation of the $50 million package is subject to certain technical and financial conditions that remain to be negotiated with Cyprus Anvil and its financial backers.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) has informed Cyprus Anvil about the Government's decision. The company will now present its mine reopening plan as accepted by the federal Government to a steering committee of Dome's main creditors within the agreement in principle. If the package is acceptable, Government and company officials will prepare a detailed agreement. The Government is optimistic that this agreement will enable the mine to re-open, and that stripping operations will commence as soon as possible.
As described in the communique issued by the Minister on April 20 in Whitehorse, the agreement was achieved after ten months of intense negotiations. Implementation which is contingent on resolution of certain financial details to protect the federal Government's investment, means the recall of 210 employees.
The Minister is convinced that this plan will result in a more competitive mine, one that will be a continuing source of stability in the coming decades for Yukon generally and for Faro in particular. He also noted that Cyprus Anvil is the bedrock of the Yukon's economy and its continued closure threatened the territory's very livelihood.
The two-year plan calls for the federal Government and Cyprus Anvil to invest $25 million each in the Faro operation. The agreement will stipulate that the federal contribution, with the exception of money Cyprus Anvil receives under existing federal programs, is fully repayable and is intended solely to re-open the Faro mine.
The Minister also paid tribute to both the Yukon Territorial Government and organized labour, whose actions helped in the efforts to re-open the mine. The Yukon Government has agreed to contribute roughly $2 million toward topping up employees' wages, plus further assistance when the mine resumes full production. In the case of organized labour, the Steelworkers Union signed a new contract boosting productivity by an estimated 20 per cent. It was also instrumental in organizing a delegation of Yukoners who supported the Minister's efforts to obtain Cabinet approval for the agreement.
The federal Government is fully aware that Cyprus Anvil is but one of many mining companies in Canada currently experiencing financial difficulty. However, Cabinet agreed that Cyprus Anvil is a unique case largely because of the federal Government's quasi-provincial responsibility in relation to Yukon's economy. Furthermore, Cyprus Anvil accounts for about 40 per cent of the territory's economic base. Failure to
act would have resulted in the Government assuming direct financial and social costs far in excess of the assistance announced.
The agreement is a symbol of what can be achieved through the co-operation of the federal and territorial Governments, business, labour and Yukoners in general.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-WAGE EQUALITY FOR WOMEN. (B) COMPILATION OF STATISTICS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-WAGE EQUALITY FOR WOMEN. (B) COMPILATION OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue a question asked of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) regarding equal pay for work of equal value, and particularly the Minister's responsibility to see that this is effected.
I should like to begin by recounting the importance of equal pay for work of equal value to the women's movement of Canada. The women's movement settled on equal pay for work of equal value as its main object in the economic field because of the inadequacy of provincial equal pay for the same job legislation. Women want to see women workers paid as men are, on the basis of skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions, according to objective criteria.
Yet, while women are ghettoized into different jobs from men, simply requiring them to have exactly the same jobs as men means that many women do not get any protection from legislation. This was a recommendation of the ILO, Convention 100 and it was taken up by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada, and recommended in 1970. Many groups lobbied for it and unions supported it after that date. Finally it was made law under the Canadian Human Rights Act. We have it on paper at least federally and we have a similar provision in Quebec for equal pay for travail equivalent.
I whould like to say that the Canadian Human Rights Commission enforces equal pay for work of equal value better than any Province enforces its equal pay legislation at the present time. But the Commission is short staffed and procees is slow. Cases take years to be investigated. The process was deliberately made to be cumbersome, and certainly when women's organizations were lobbying for it they wanted to see it speeded up. There is a complaint stage, an investigation stage and a separate conciliation stage; all this takes an enormous amount of time.
The difficulty is, Mr. Speaker, that the wrong problem is addressed. The model is wrong. Equal pay for work of equal value treats discrimination as an anomoly; that there is an exception when women are paid less than men for doing whatever their job is. This is seen as a failure in human relations. If we could only get the employer and employee together, then we could have reason prevail.
The human rights model, which I would suggest is the incorrect model for labour relations is a model which has worked best for landlord and tenant relations, particularly to
April 25, 1983

get a landlord to accept a tenant of a minority racial or ethnic group. The point is, however, the landlord will be getting the same rent when he does this.
The difference here with equal pay for work of equal value is that paying women less is profitable for companies. The employer will make more money if he can hire women workers who will do the work for less money than male workers. Therefore, it is not a failure of good will, but simply economics.
There is a growing library of literature which shows as well that equal pay legislation at the provincial level has not been successful. That is the case-by-case approach which the Canadian Human Rights Act also uses. Let me give you a few statistics for wages and salaries for full-year employees for all of Canada.
In 1969 women's wages and salaries on average as a per cent of men's salaries was 55.6 per cent; in 1971 it was 55.3 per cent; in 1973 it was 55.8 per cent; in 1975 it was 56.1 per cent; and in 1977 it was up to 57.8 per cent. The latest year for which we have statistics available is 1980, and then the percentage was 58.3. All of these figures are under 60 per cent. The figures fluctuate a little from year to year so that I do not even think we can be enthusiastic that we have gone up from 55 per cent to 58 per cent. We are not sure that this is a lasting increase or just one of the fluctuations; that figure may have gone down in the following year.
Women, therefore, are earning somewhat under 60 per cent of men's wages and salaries for full-time work. Studies show that roughly half of this 40 per cent difference can be attributed to women being paid less than men for doing the same job, and roughly half because they are doing different work. If provincial legislation were working, we would see that women would be earning about 80 per cent of what men do. That is, they would be receiving this 80 per cent figure and the other 20 per cent would be because of women being in job ghettos.
If the federal legislation were working however, that is equal pay for work of equal value, women would be earning on average the same, roughly 100 per cent of what men are earning. And if the federal legislation were working, we would see that wage and salary gap for federal employees declining, and we would see it decline, but not as fast, for provincial employees. If the Minister of Labour had relevant statistics it would be possible to look at this. I do not believe there are any such statistics, and that is regrettable. There should be. The Minister of Labour should be able to show this. If he wants to argue, as he did in replying to me, that the Canadian Human Rights Act is such a good thing, he should show that the gap is declining for people who are under this legislation.
I suggest it is very clear that the legislation is not effective and that there is a lot more that can be done. I suggest that the Minister of Labour himself has some responsibility. It is not enough to say that 90 per cent of Canadian workers are under provincial jurisdiction. He should still be doing something for those 10 per cent of Canadian women workers who come under his jurisdiction. Furthermore, the Canada Labour Code specifies what the Ministry of Labour can do. In Part III,
Adjournment Debate
Division 11.1, Section 38.1(1) we learn that employers are required to live up to the same expectations of Section 11 of the Canadian Human Rights Act. I will quote from Section 38.1(2):
Where an inspector has reasonable grounds at any time for believing that an employer is engaging or has engaged in a discriminatory practice described in subsection (1), the inspector may notify the Canadian Human Rights Commission or file a complaint with the Commission-
In other words, inspectors could be filing complaints. But are they? In 1981 there were only one or two filed by inspectors and we have 127 labour inspectors in Canada for all provisions of the Code. No complaints were filed in 1982. The Department of Labour, Women's Bureau, had an ad campaign on equal pay, but it did not have a phone-in number. It did not facilitate complaints. They had a campaign on sexual harassment and they received a lot of phone calls. I suggest they should be welcoming phone calls and they should be acting on them, taking up complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
I would like to suggest further that the Minister could be helping the women's movement and union groups which are working for equal pay for work of equal value. These people need statistics as part of their campaign. Instead of doing this, however, we see the Ministry of Labour, which does publish material, not publishing what it should.
This book, "Facts and Figures", is an old and useful handbook which is no longer available in this form. There were complaints that it was not useful enough because it was inconsistent. Instead, what we have now is a glorified computer print-out. We also have discontinued series, Mr. Speaker, for average weekly and hourly earnings. They were extremely useful statistics. They showed a long and stable wage and salary gap. The Department of Labour discontinued this series.
To conclude, I would like to suggest that if the Minister is concerned about equal pay for work of equal value, and if he is concerned about justice for Canadian women workers, there is a lot he could be doing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-WAGE EQUALITY FOR WOMEN. (B) COMPILATION OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) is very much committed to the policy of equal pay for work of equal value. That is the policy of this Government and always has been. We as the Government, and I know the Minister of Labour, are anxiously waiting for the day when, not only in the public service but in the private sector, the philosophy practiced will be equal pay for work of equal value.
Judging by the original question of the Hon. Member and by her remarks today, she seems to imply that Labour Canada has discontinued its annual survey of wages in Canadian industry. In fact, the Labour Data Branch has conducted surveys annually since at least 1974, and continues to publish the results annually in the publication "Wage Rates, Salaries

April 25, 1983
Adjournment Debate
and Hours of Labour". This report presents information on wage rates and salaries for selected cross-industry and specific industry occupations by sex and union status. Information pertaining to the standard hours of work for office and nonoffice employees is also shown.
"Wage Rates, Salaries and Hours of Labour" is published separately for Canada as a whole and for selected Canadian cities, including St. John's, Charlottetown, Trois-Rivieres, Saskatoon, Regina, Victoria, Saint John, Halifax-Dartmouth, St. Catharines-Niagara, Ottawa-Hull, Thunder Bay, Kitchen-er-Waterloo, Windsor, London-St.Thomas, Vancouver, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton, Quebec City, Montreal and Toronto. As the Hon. Members can see, no city is omitted.
In addition, the Women's Bureau of Labour Canada annually publishes a three part report entitled "Women in the Labour
Lorce". Part 1 deals with participation rates of women. Part 2 is entitled "Earnings of Men and Women", and provides data on male-female earnings by sex, age, occupation and education. These data are obtained from surveys conducted by Statistics Canada and, as mentioned, from Labour Canada. Part 3 of the report provides a variety of facts and figures on such issues as unionization, pensions, day care, and complaints of discrimination on the basis of sex, as registered with the Human Rights Commission.
